1.pericope_label: Faith is the substance of things hoped for: the definition, and the witness borne to the elders

schools.summary: Gill insists on identifying which faith is meant: not a mere moral virtue, which is a branch of the law, nor a bare assent to anything revealed and affirmed in the Gospel, nor a faith of doing miracles, nor an implicit one, nor a mere profession which is sometimes temporary, nor the word or doctrine of faith, but that mentioned in the preceding chapter by which the just man lives and which has the salvation of the soul annexed to it. It does not so much design any particular branch or act of faith as that which in general respects the various promises and blessings of grace, and it chiefly regards the faith of Old Testament saints, though that is the same in nature, object and acts as the faith of New Testament ones, being a firm persuasion of the power, faithfulness and love of God in Christ. By the elders he understands not merely old men or elders in age but such as lived in ancient times, some before the flood and to a great age, others in office civil or ecclesiastical, the ancestors and predecessors of the Hebrews; these obtained a good report from God, that they were his chosen and were justified and accepted with him, and from men, from the good for their faith and holiness and from the evil for their good works. Calvin opens by protesting the chapter division: whoever made this the beginning of the eleventh chapter has unwisely disjointed the context, since the object of the Apostle was to prove what he had already said, that there is need of patience, and Griesbach makes the division at the thirty-eighth verse of the last chapter, which is no doubt what the subject requires. Having quoted the testimony of Habakkuk that the just lives by faith, the Apostle now shows that faith can be no more separated from patience than from itself: we shall not reach the goal of salvation except we have patience, for faith directs us to things afar off which we do not as yet enjoy, and so necessarily includes patience. From this Calvin draws his sharpest point, that those are greatly mistaken who think an exact definition of faith is given here, since the Apostle does not speak of the whole of what faith is but selects that part of it which was suitable to his purpose. On the first term he presses the paradox: we know that what we hope for is not what we have as it were in hand but what is as yet hid from us, or at least the enjoyment of which is delayed to another time, so that faith regards not present things but such as are waited for, and this kind of contradiction is not without its force and beauty. On the elders he prefers the rendering of Macknight and Stuart, ancients, as more suitable in our language, since the word elders most commonly refers to age but ancients to time, those meant being such as lived before and under the Law; and he explains that the fathers obtained salvation and were accepted by God in no other way than by faith, a point the Jews needed, since a foolish admiration of the fathers had so prevailed among them that it proved a great hindrance to a thorough surrender of themselves to Christ and to his government, occasioned by ambition or superstition or both, so that hearing they were the blessed and holy seed of Abraham they fixed their eyes on men rather than on God.

Henry gives a definition or description of the grace of faith in two parts. First, it is the substance of things hoped for: faith and hope go together, and the same things that are the object of our hope are the object of our faith; it is a firm persuasion and expectation that God will perform all that he has promised to us in Christ, and this persuasion is so strong that it gives the soul a kind of possession and present fruition of those things, gives them a subsistence in the soul by the first-fruits and foretastes of them, so that believers in the exercise of faith are filled with joy unspeakable and full of glory. Christ dwells in the soul by faith, and the soul is filled with the fullness of God as far as its present measure will admit, experiencing a substantial reality in the objects of faith. Second, it is the evidence of things not seen: faith demonstrates to the eye of the mind the reality of those things that cannot be discerned by the eye of the body, and is the firm assent of the soul to the divine revelation and every part of it, set home upon the mind by the blessed Spirit and received by the spiritual understanding. Henry adds that faith is the leading grace to all the rest, and that the chapter which follows is an illustration of what faith has enabled the people of God to do, to bear, and to hope for; the honour done to the elders was done to their faith, and what they obtained they obtained by believing.

Clarke opens with an analysis of the whole chapter, tracing the definition of faith, its immediate objects, and its effects instanced in Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sara, their righteous posterity, the offering of Isaac, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the Israelites in the wilderness, the fall of Jericho, Rahab, several of the judges and David and Samuel and the prophets, and finally the glorious effects produced by it in the primitive martyrs. On the first term he renders it the subsistence of things hoped for, explaining that the word signifies subsistence, that which becomes a foundation for another thing to stand on. On the second he says it signifies such a conviction as is produced in the mind by the demonstration of a problem, after which demonstration no doubt can remain, because we see from it that the thing is, that it cannot but be, and that it cannot be otherwise than as it is and is proved to be; such is the faith by which the soul is justified, or rather such are the effects of justifying faith, on which subsists the peace of God that passes all understanding, while the love of God is shed abroad in the heart by the Holy Ghost and the Spirit witnesses with their spirits that their sins are blotted out, as fully manifest to their judgment and conscience as the axioms that a whole is greater than any of its parts and that equal lines and angles placed on one another do not exceed each other, or the deduction that the square of the base of a right-angled triangle equals the squares of the other two sides. On the elders he takes them as ancestors and forefathers, the patriarchs and prophets, and remarks what is missing: it is very remarkable that among the whole there is not one word concerning poor Adam and his wife, though both Abraham and Sarah are mentioned, and there was no good report concerning them, not a word of their repentance, faith or holiness; had there been anything praiseworthy in their life after the fall, any act of faith by which they could have been distinguished, it would surely have come out here, since the mention of their second son Abel would have suggested it, but God has covered the whole of their spiritual and eternal state with a thick and impenetrable veil. Wesley holds that the definition given in this verse, and exemplified in the various instances following, undoubtedly includes justifying faith but not directly as justifying, for faith justifies only as it refers to and depends on Christ, and here is no mention of him as the object of faith, while in several of the instances that follow no notice is taken of him or his salvation but only of temporal blessings obtained by faith; yet they may all be considered as evidences of the power of justifying faith in Christ and of its extensive exercise in a course of steady obedience amidst difficulties and dangers of every kind. He renders the verse as the subsistence of things hoped for and the evidence or conviction of things not seen, and distinguishes the two halves carefully: things hoped for are not so extensive as things not seen, the former being only things future and joyful to us while the latter are either future, past or present, and those either joyful or terrible. On the elders he calls the chapter a kind of summary of the Old Testament, in which the apostle comprises the designs, labours, sojournings, expectations, temptations and martyrdoms of the ancients, the former of them having a long exercise of their patience and the latter suffering shorter but sharper trials; and of the testimony he says it is a most comprehensive word, since God gave a testimony not only of them but to them, and they received his testimony as if it had been the things themselves of which he testified, whence they also gave testimony to others and others testified of them.

Barnes prefixes an analysis of the chapter to his comment. In the close of the previous chapter the apostle had incidentally made mention of faith and said that the just should live by faith; the object of the whole argument in the epistle was to keep those addressed from apostatising from the Christian religion and especially from relapsing again into Judaism, since they were in the midst of trials and evidently suffering some form of persecution which tended to expose them to that danger. The indispensable means of securing them from apostasy was faith, and to show its efficacy the apostle goes into an extended account of its nature and effects occupying the entire chapter; and as the persons addressed had been Hebrews, and as the Old Testament contained numerous instances of persons in substantially the same circumstances, the reference is made to the illustrious examples of the efficacy of faith in the Jewish history, to show that confidence in the divine promises has been in all ages the means of perseverance in the true religion and consequently of salvation. On the elders he takes them as the ancients, the Hebrew patriarchs and fathers, and renders the phrase literally as were witnessed of, an honourable testimony having been borne to them in consequence of their faith; the idea is that their acting under the influence of faith in the circumstances in which they were was the ground of the honourable testimony borne to them in the Old Testament, and in the cases he proceeds to enumerate he mentions those whose piety is particularly commended there and who showed in trying circumstances that they had unwavering confidence in God. Ellicott sets the verse in the movement of the epistle: the coming of the Lord for judgment upon his adversaries and salvation to his people draws nigh, in the midst of dangers and judgments God’s righteous servant shall live, and the ground of his life is his steadfast faith, so that our principle of action is not shrinking back but faith. He reports the debate whether what follows is a definition of what faith is or a description of what faith does, and answers that it is not a complete definition in the sense of including all the moments of thought present in the word as used in the last chapter or in this, but that the things hoped for are not mere figments of the imagination since their basis is the word of God; if that is kept in mind the words agree with all that has led up to them and with all that follows, and whether they be called definition or description will be of little consequence. The exact meaning of the special terms he says it is not easy to ascertain: the word rendered substance has already occurred twice in the epistle, first in its true meaning of the essence which so to speak stands under the qualities possessed, and then with the same metaphor of standing under applied to steadfastness or confidence; the Authorised version here deserted the earlier translations, which for the most part have sure confidence or ground, to follow the Rhemish in its rendering of the Latin, but the sense so presented is not very clear, and the symmetry of the verse almost compels us to choose some word denoting an act or at all events an attitude of the mind. On the second verse he renders it better as for therein the elders had witness borne to them, and takes the connection to be that faith truly accomplishes all this, since it was in the exercise of such a faith that the elders gained the witness which the Scripture bears to them and to their noble deeds, the verse being added to confirm the first. Robertson notes that the writer has just said we are of faith, not of apostasy, and now proceeds in a chapter of great eloquence and passion to illustrate his point by a recital of the heroes of faith whose example should spur his readers to like loyalty. The first term he traces as a very common word from Aristotle on, from a verb meaning to stand under, denoting what stands under anything such as a building, a contract or a promise; he points to its philosophical use in the first chapter and its sense of assurance and steadiness of mind elsewhere, and observes that it is common in the papyri in business documents as the basis or guarantee of transactions, which suggests a rendering along those lines here. On the elders he takes the demonstrative as referring back to faith, notes that the word is more nearly like the fathers than the technical sense of elders as officers usual in the New Testament, comparing the tradition of the elders, and parses the closing verb as a first aorist passive, were testified to.

debates: Whether the opening sentence is a definition of faith: Calvin denies it outright, holding that the Apostle selects only the part of faith suited to his argument about patience, Ellicott reports the debate and settles it by calling the distinction of little consequence once the ground in God’s word is granted, and Henry and Clarke both treat the sentence as a working definition in two parts

How the word rendered substance should be taken: Clarke and Henry keep the sense of a foundation or subsistence in the soul, Ellicott argues that the Authorised rendering follows the Latin against the earlier English versions and that the symmetry of the verse demands a word denoting an act of the mind, and Robertson turns to the papyri where the word guarantees a business transaction
Where the chapter should begin: Calvin follows Griesbach in putting the division three verses earlier, since the argument from Habakkuk about patience runs straight on into the sentence about faith
outliers: Clarke supports the sense of the second term from geometry, the axioms about wholes and parts and the theorem on the square of the hypotenuse
Clarke observes that Adam and Eve are the one conspicuous absence from the roll of the faithful, their state covered with an impenetrable veil
Calvin diagnoses a Jewish admiration of the fathers so inflated that it hindered surrender to Christ
Wesley distinguishes things hoped for, which are future and joyful, from things not seen, which may be past or present and terrible

3.pericope_label: Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God

schools.summary: Chrysostom prefaces the roll of examples with an account of what faith demands. Faith needs a generous and vigorous soul, one rising above all things of sense and passing beyond the weakness of human reasonings, for it is not possible to become a believer otherwise than by raising oneself above the common customs of the world. He then explains why the writer proceeds as he does. The souls of the Hebrews were thoroughly weakened; though they had begun from faith, yet from circumstances, that is from sufferings and afflictions, they had afterwards become faint-hearted and of little spirit and were shaken from their position. The writer therefore encouraged them first from these very things, bidding them call to remembrance the former days; next from the Scripture which says that the just shall live by faith; afterwards from arguments, saying that faith is the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen; and now again from their forefathers, those great and admirable men. Chrysostom presses the comparison the argument implies: if those who lived when the good things were far off and the promises unfulfilled were nevertheless saved by faith and bore what they bore, much more should those to whom the good things have come near hold fast without wavering, since it would be shameful to fall short of men who had so much less light and so much longer to wait.

Gill enumerates what the plural takes in: the celestial world with its inhabitants the angels, the starry and ethereal worlds with all that is in them, the sun and moon and stars and the fowls of the air, the terrestrial world with all upon it, men and beasts and the rest, and the watery world, the sea and all that is therein. He allows that some respect may be had to the distinction of worlds among the Jews, but denies that the apostle can be thought to have any regard to their extravagant notions of vast numbers of worlds being created; they often speak of three hundred and ten worlds, in all of which they say there are heavens, earth, stars and planets, and sometimes of eighteen thousand, but these notions are rightly charged by Philo with ignorance and folly. However many worlds there are, he says, they are made by the Word of God, by Christ the essential Word to whom the creation of all things is ascribed. Calvin takes the sense to be that we, by faith in God’s word which gives the record, understand or know how the world was made; this the heathens did not know by the light of reason, and yet they might have known it, so that the reference here is to the fact as it was while the parallel passage speaks of what ought to have been the case. On the plural he reports that the same word, though in the plural number, is rendered as a singular elsewhere, and so here by Beza and others, since the universe, the whole visible creation, is what is meant, as appears from the word seen in the next clause; he cites Stuart that the singular is not employed to designate the world in the sense of the universe, the plural being used to express the various parts of which the world is composed, though he observes that our own term world already comprehends the whole visible creation. He notes further that Beza renders the verb framed as compacted, and that the point of the whole is that the invisible power of God is to be seen in the visible fabric, so that what is set before the eyes had its origin in what no eye can see.

Clarke argues from the terms. By worlds we are to understand the material fabric of the universe, for the word can have no reference here to age or any measurement of time, since the writer speaks of the things which are seen as not being made out of the things which do appear, and this must therefore refer to the material creation; and as the word is used in the plural number it may comprehend not only the earth and visible heavens but the whole planetary system, the different worlds which in our system at least revolve round the sun. On the last clause he presses a close argument: the apostle states that these things were not made out of a pre-existent matter, for if they were, that matter, however extended or modified, must appear in that thing into which it is compounded and modified, and consequently it could not be said that the things which are seen are not made of the things that appear. He shows us also by these words, Clarke adds, that the present mundane fabric was not formed or reformed from one anterior to it, as some suppose. Wesley takes the worlds as heaven and earth and all things in them, visible and invisible, and the verb as meaning formed, fashioned and finished, by the word, that is by the sole command of God without any instrument or preceding matter. He draws from this the principle that as creation is the foundation and specimen of the whole divine economy, so faith in the creation is the foundation and specimen of all faith. On the last clause he grants a chaos but refuses it any independence: the things which are seen, as the sun and earth and stars, were made of things which do not appear, out of the dark, unapparent chaos of the second verse of Genesis, and this very chaos was itself created by the divine power, for before it was thus created it had no existence in nature.

Barnes explains why this is the first instance of the strength of faith to which the apostle refers, namely that by which we give credence to the declarations of the Scriptures about the work of creation. It is selected first evidently because it is the first thing that occurs in the Bible, or the first thing narrated there in relation to which there is the exercise of faith; he points to no particular instance in which this faith was exercised, for none is especially mentioned, but refers to it as an illustration of the nature of faith which every one might observe in himself. The faith here exercised is confidence in the truth of the divine declarations in regard to the creation, and the meaning is that our knowledge on this subject is a mere matter of faith in the divine testimony: it is not that we could reason this out and demonstrate that the worlds were thus made, nor that profane history goes back to that period and informs us of it. Ellicott prefers the rendering by faith, as in the following verses, and notes that the first place is not given to the elders because the writer’s object is to set forth the achievements of faith, with which he would say the Scripture record is filled; even where there is no mention of this principle we must trace it in the lives of God’s servants, and even where there is no history of men there is a necessity for the exercise of faith by ourselves, which the first words of Scripture teach. He renders the clause literally as that the ages have been prepared, noting that the remarkable expression used in the first chapter is here repeated, and takes the idea presented by the words to be the complete preparation of all that the successive periods of time contain; the narrative of the first chapter of Genesis ascribes the whole creation of the heaven and the earth to God and associates a word of God with every stage in the preparation and furnishing of the earth. Robertson parses the instrumental case of the noun for faith and observes that each example as far as the mention of Rahab is formally and with rhetorical skill introduced by that same phrase, after which only a summary is given. He parses the verb for understanding as a present active indicative of an old verb derived from the word for intellect, and says the author appeals to our knowledge of the world in which these heroes lived as an illustration of faith, adding that recent books by great scientists confirm the position here taken that a Supreme Mind is behind and before the universe, and that science can only stand still in God’s presence and believe like a little child. The worlds he renders as the ages, comparing the earlier use in the epistle, and takes the noun as an accusative of general reference; the verb he parses as a perfect passive infinitive of a verb meaning to mend, to equip or to perfect, standing in indirect discourse after the verb of understanding.

debates: What the plural rendered worlds means: Clarke insists it cannot mean ages here since the contrast is with things seen, and takes it of the material universe and perhaps the whole planetary system, Ellicott renders it literally as the ages and finds in it the complete preparation of all that successive periods of time contain, Calvin reports Beza and others rendering it as a simple singular and cites Stuart on the usage, and Robertson keeps the ages while noting the accusative of general reference

Whether creation was from pre-existent matter: Clarke argues that if it were, the matter would necessarily appear in the compound, so that the clause would be false, and adds that the present fabric was not reformed from an anterior one, while Wesley allows a chaos but insists it was itself created and had no prior existence in nature

Why this example stands first in the roll: Barnes says because it is the first thing in the Bible calling for faith, Ellicott because the writer means to show that faith is required of us even where there is no history of men to record it, and Chrysostom because the readers, weakened by suffering, needed the argument carried back to their forefathers
outliers: Gill reports and dismisses the rabbinic reckoning of three hundred and ten worlds, and sometimes eighteen thousand, on Philo’s authority
Robertson appeals to contemporary physics for a Supreme Mind behind the universe, and bids science believe like a little child
Wesley makes faith in the creation the foundation and specimen of all faith
Chrysostom describes the readers as men who began from faith but were shaken from their position by affliction

4.pericope_label: By faith Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice, and being dead yet speaketh

schools.summary: Gill begins by asking why Adam and Eve are passed over, and answers that this omission is not because they were not believers, but either because of the fall and ruin of mankind by them, or because the apostle speaks only of such as had received some eminent testimony by faith, passing by many believers and hastening to Abraham the father of the Jews. The superior excellency of Abel’s sacrifice to Cain’s he locates both in the matter and in the manner of it: the one was offered heartily to the Lord and the other only in show, the one was offered in faith and the other not, and Abel looked through his sacrifice to the sacrifice of Christ while Cain did not. He presses the typology in detail: Abel’s sacrifice was a lamb, a type of Christ the Lamb of God; a firstling, a figure of him who is the firstborn of every creature; one of the fattest of his flock, expressive of the excellency of Christ; and it was offered up at the end of days, as Christ was offered at the end of the world. The testimony God gave he takes as a declaration of Abel’s righteousness, not that his sacrifice made him righteous but that it declared him to be so, his person being first accepted and then his gift; and the speaking after death he refers both to the crying of his blood from the ground and to the continuing witness of his example, by which he still teaches the church the way of acceptable worship. Calvin states the governing thesis of the whole chapter: the Apostle’s object is to show that however excellent were the works of the saints, it was from faith that they derived their value, their worthiness and all their excellences, and hence that the fathers pleased God by faith alone. He commends faith here on two accounts, that it renders obedience to God, attempting and undertaking nothing but what is according to the rule of God’s word, and that it relies on God’s promises and so gains for works the value and worth which belongs to them from grace alone; wherever the word faith occurs in this chapter we must bear in mind that the Apostle speaks of it in order that the Jews might regard no other rule than God’s word and depend alone on his promises. On Abel he is uncompromising: his sacrifice was for no other reason preferable to that of his brother except that it was sanctified by faith. He notes that the word for sacrifice properly means an offered victim but sometimes anything offered to God, Abel’s being called an offering in Genesis, and that the comparative is literally more but is used of number, quantity or excellency, the last being evidently the meaning here since Abel’s offering was distinguished not in number or quantity but in quality, so that a better or more excellent sacrifice is the sense and not a fuller one.

Henry divides the examples that follow into two classes, those whose names are mentioned and the particular exercise and actings of whose faith are specified, and those whose names are barely mentioned with an account given in general of the exploits of their faith, which the reader is left to accommodate to the particular persons from the sacred story. On the silence about our first parents he observes that the Spirit of God has not thought fit to say anything here of their faith, and yet the church of God has generally, by a pious charity, taken it for granted that God gave them repentance and faith in the promised seed, that he instructed them in the mystery of sacrificing, that they instructed their children in it, and that they found mercy with God after they had ruined themselves and all their posterity; but God has left the matter still under some doubt, as a warning to all who have great talents given to them and a great trust reposed in them that they do not prove unfaithful, since God would not enroll our first parents among the number of believers in this blessed calendar. The list begins instead with Abel, one of the first saints and the first martyr for religion of all the sons of Adam, one who lived by faith and died for it, and therefore a fit pattern for the Hebrews to imitate. What Abel did by faith Henry describes as offering a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, a more full and perfect sacrifice, and from this he draws several lessons: that after the fall God opened a new way for the children of men to return to him in religious worship, this being one of the first instances upon record of fallen men going in to worship God and a wonder of mercy that all intercourse between God and man was not cut off by the fall; that after the fall God must be worshipped by sacrifices, a way of worship which carries in it a confession of sin and of the desert of sin and a profession of faith in a Redeemer who was to be a ransom for the souls of men; and that from the beginning there has been a remarkable difference between the worshippers. Here were two persons, brethren, both of whom went in to worship God, and yet there was a vast difference: Cain was the elder brother but Abel has the preference, since it is not seniority of birth but grace that makes men truly honourable. The difference Henry finds observable in their persons, Abel being an upright person, a righteous man and a true believer while Cain was a formalist who had not a principle of special grace, and observable also in their principles, since Abel acted under the power of faith while Cain acted only from the force of education or natural conscience.

Clarke takes the comparative in its most literal sense, more sacrifice, as if the writer had said that Abel by faith made more than one offering, which is why it is added that God testified of his gifts in the plural. The plain state of the case, he thinks, was this: Cain and Abel both brought offerings to the altar of God, probably the altar erected for the family worship; as Cain was a husbandman he brought a eucharistic offering of the fruits of the ground, by which he acknowledged the being and providence of God, while Abel, being a shepherd or feeder of cattle, brought not only the eucharistic offering but also of the produce of his flock as a sin-offering, by which he acknowledged his own sinfulness and God’s justice and mercy as well as his being and providence. Cain, not at all apprehensive of the demerit of sin or of God’s holiness, contented himself with the thank-offering, which God could not consistently with his holiness and justice receive with complacency, while the other, as referring to him who was the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, God could receive and did particularly testify his approbation of; and though the eucharistic offering was a very proper offering in its place, this one was not received because there was no sin-offering with it. On the last clause Clarke says that by this faith, thus exercised in reference to an atonement, Abel though dead yet speaketh, that is, preaches to mankind the necessity of an atonement and the acceptance of the sinner through it. Wesley takes the faith to be faith in the future Redeemer, and the more excellent sacrifice to be the firstlings of Abel’s flock, implying both a confession of what his own sins deserved and a desire of sharing in the great atonement, whereas Cain’s offering testified no such faith but only a bare acknowledgment of God the Creator. By that faith, he says, Abel obtained both righteousness and a testimony of it, God testifying visibly that his gifts were accepted, probably by sending fire from heaven to consume his sacrifice, a token that justice seized on the sacrifice instead of the sinner who offered it; and being dead he yet speaketh this, that a sinner is accepted only through faith in the great sacrifice.

Barnes notes at the outset that in the account in Genesis of the offering made by Abel there is no mention of faith, as is true also of most of the instances referred to by the apostle, the narrative saying simply that Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof and that the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering. Men have speculated much as to the reason why the offering of Abel was accepted and that of Cain rejected, but such speculation rests on no certain basis, and the solution of the apostle should be regarded as decisive and satisfactory, that in the one case there was faith and in the other not. It could not have been because an offering of the fruits of the ground was not pleasing to God, for such an offering was commanded under the Jewish law and was not in itself improper; both the brothers selected that which was to them most obvious, which they had reared with their own hands and regarded as most valuable, Cain having cultivated the earth and naturally bringing what had grown under his care while Abel kept a flock and as naturally brought what he had raised. Had the temper of mind in both been the same, Barnes concludes, there is no reason to doubt that the offering of each would have been accepted, and to this conclusion we are led by the nature of the case, the apostle advancing substantially the same sentiment when he says that the particular state of mind on which the whole turned was that the one had faith and the other had not. Ellicott observes that the Greek literally means that Abel’s sacrifice was more than Cain’s, comparing similar uses elsewhere, and that the word rendered sacrifice, which like very many words in this chapter is taken directly from the Greek version, has not its special sense here, since in the narrative of Genesis the offerings of the two brothers are designated by the same name both in the Hebrew and in the Greek. Hence, apart from the first words by faith, there is nothing here said to explain the superiority of Abel’s offering, though one who believes sacrifice to have been of divine institution, and who notes the close connection between God’s word and the actions of the men whose faith is here recorded, may hold it probable that Abel’s obedience was manifested in his mode of approaching God. On the witness he says it is probably through which faith, though the Greek may also mean through which sacrifice, and takes the witness to be that borne by God in his acceptance of the offering, shown by some visible sign; he adds that such a testimony to Abel is implied in the reproof of Cain, but that the following words about God bearing witness in regard to his gifts show what was chiefly in the writer’s thought, and that such acceptance implied Abel’s righteousness and thus testified to his faith. Robertson parses the comparative as literally more sacrifice, noting this rather free use of the word with the point implied rather than stated and citing parallels, and explains the construction of the comparison after the preposition. He parses the verb of witness as a first aorist passive as in the earlier verse, he was witnessed to, and the infinitive that follows as indirect discourse with a personal construction, the predicate adjective agreeing with the subject of the passive verb; the clause about God is a genitive absolute with a present active participle. Like Ellicott he refuses to go beyond the text, saying that precisely why Abel’s sacrifice was better than that of Cain, apart from his faith, is not shown; and the closing participle he parses as a second aorist active, having died, with the present tense of the verb of speaking meaning that Abel speaks still through his faith.

debates: Why Abel’s sacrifice was accepted and Cain’s refused: Calvin allows only that it was sanctified by faith and settles the comparative on quality rather than quantity, Robertson and Ellicott both say the text does not disclose any further reason, and Barnes argues positively that an offering of the fruits of the ground could not have been displeasing since the law afterwards commanded it, while Clarke, Wesley and Gill all find the difference in the offering itself, Clarke taking the comparative as more sacrifice and reconstructing a eucharistic offering to which Abel alone added a sin-offering

Whether Adam and Eve are deliberately omitted: Gill offers two reasons, the ruin of mankind by them and the apostle’s restriction to those who received eminent testimony, while Henry treats the silence as a standing warning to those entrusted with great talents, and Clarke elsewhere calls their state covered with an impenetrable veil

What the testimony God bore consisted in: Ellicott says some visible sign accompanying the acceptance, Wesley guesses fire from heaven consuming the sacrifice as a token that justice seized the victim instead of the sinner, and Robertson keeps to the grammar, that Abel himself was witnessed to as righteous
outliers: Gill reads Abel’s lamb, its being a firstling, its fatness and the season of its offering as four distinct types of Christ
Henry calls Abel the first martyr for religion of all the sons of Adam, one who lived by faith and died for it
Clarke has Abel still preaching the necessity of an atonement to mankind
Barnes points out that the Genesis narrative never mentions faith at all, here or in most of the chapter’s other instances

5.pericope_label: By faith Enoch was translated; and without faith it is impossible to please God

schools.summary: Gill defines the translation by ruling out what it was not: it is to be understood not of a spiritual translation from the power of darkness into the kingdom of Christ, as all converted persons are translated and as Enoch doubtless was, nor of a rapture or removal from one part of the earth to another or from one part of a country to another, as Philip was caught away by the Spirit after the baptism of the eunuch, but of a translation from earth to heaven; and not for a while only, as Paul was caught up to the third heaven, but as Elijah was, there to continue, and as the living saints will be at the last day. It was a translation of him soul and body to heaven, to eternal glory and happiness, by a change from mortality to immortality which passed upon him, and which is a pledge of the resurrection. On the following verse he guards the negative: without faith it is impossible to please God or to do things well pleasing in his sight, or any of the duties of religion in an acceptable way, whether prayer, praise, attendance on the word and ordinances, or any good works whatever, because such things are done without Christ and without his Spirit and have neither right principles nor right ends. But he adds a careful qualification, that this is not to be understood of the persons of God’s elect as considered in Christ, in whom they are well pleasing to him before faith, being loved with an everlasting love and chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world. Calvin observes that the writer chose a few of the most ancient examples in order to make a transition to Abraham and his posterity, and then asks the question the others pass over, why God in so unusual a manner removed Enoch from the earth. The event was remarkable, and hence all may know how dear he was to God; impiety and all kinds of corruptions then prevailed everywhere, and had he died as other men it would not have occurred to any that he was preserved from the prevailing contagion by God’s providence, but as he was taken away without dying the hand of God from heaven, removing him as it were from the fire, was openly manifested. It was therefore no ordinary honour with which God had favoured him, and though Moses tells us only that he was a righteous man, the writer of the epistle supplies what the narrative leaves implicit, that the root of that righteousness was faith. On the following verse Calvin says what is said there belongs to all the examples recorded in the chapter, and that since the passage has some measure of obscurity its meaning must be examined more closely, there being no better interpreter than the Apostle himself: the proof immediately subjoined serves as the explanation. The reason he assigns why no one can please God without faith is that no one will ever come to God except he believes that God is and is also convinced that he is a remunerator to all who seek him; and if access to God is not opened but by faith, it follows that all who are without it are the objects of God’s displeasure. Hence the Apostle shows how faith obtains favour for us, even because faith is our teacher as to the true worship of God, and because it makes us certain that our obedience is pleasing to him and our service not spent in vain.

Clarke keeps to the plain point that the apostle is explaining what the phrase in Genesis means: it is said there that Enoch walked with God and he was not, for God took him, and here the apostle explains God’s taking him by saying that he was translated that he should not see death, from which we learn that he did not die and that God took him to a state of blessedness without obliging him to pass through death. On the following verse he sets out at length what the worshipper must hold. The man who professes that it is his duty to worship God must, if he act rationally, do it on the conviction that there is such a Being, infinite, eternal, unoriginated and self-existent, the cause of all other being, on whom all being depends, and by whose energy and bounty and providence all other beings exist and live and are supplied with the means of continued existence and life. He must believe also that God rewards them that diligently seek him, that he is not indifferent about his own worship, that he requires adoration and religious service from men, and that he blesses and especially protects and saves those who in simplicity and uprightness of heart seek and serve him; and this requires faith, such a faith as has already been described, a faith by which we can please God. Wesley adds to the account of Enoch only that he was no longer found among men, though perhaps they sought for him as they did for Elijah, and that the testimony he had was from God in his own conscience. On the following verse he is equally brief, saying that even some divine faith in God is necessary, since he that cometh to God in prayer or another act of worship must believe that he is.

Barnes notes that the account of Enoch in Genesis is very brief, that he walked with God and he was not, for God took him, and that there is no particular mention there of his faith. The apostle attributes it to him, as in the case of Abel, either because faith was involved in the very nature of piety or because the fact was communicated to him by direct revelation; but there is nothing in the Genesis account inconsistent with the belief that Enoch was characterised by eminent faith, which is rather implied in the expression that he walked with God, and may also be implied in what is said by the apostle Jude, that he prophesied of the Lord coming with ten thousand of his saints. On the following verse Barnes generalises the principle far beyond religion: without confidence in God, in his fidelity, his truth, his wisdom and his promises, it is impossible to please him, and this is as true in other things as in religion. It is impossible for a child to please his father unless he has confidence in him, or for a wife to please her husband or a husband a wife unless they have confidence in each other, for if there is distrust and jealousy on either part there is discord and misery; we cannot be pleased with a professed friend unless he has such confidence in us as to believe our declarations and promises, and the same thing is true of God, who cannot be pleased with the man who has no confidence in him, who doubts the truth of his declarations and promises, and who does not believe that his ways are right. Ellicott points out that the words are an exact quotation from the Greek version of Genesis, and that the word rendered translated is a very simple one denoting merely change of place, but that nothing can equal the simplicity of the Hebrew, he was not, for God took him. He renders the testimony better as he hath had witness borne to him that he hath been well pleasing to God, and observes that the form of the expression shows the writer is again speaking of the ever present word of Scripture: that word does not record the translation of Enoch until it hath borne witness to him that he pleased God, the Hebrew words walked with God being rendered in the Greek version as was well pleasing to God, and it is this rendering that is quoted. On the following verse he prefers apart from faith it is impossible to be well pleasing unto him, for he that draweth near to God must believe, and draws the inference backwards: the very statement that Enoch pleased God is an assertion that in him faith was found, and no one can be the habitual worshipper of God, which is what the phrase implies, if his faith does not grasp these two truths. The second he renders literally as becometh a recompenser, since the future recompense is present to the eye of faith. Robertson parses the verb of translation as a first aorist passive of an old verb meaning to transpose or to change, notes that the same verb recurs immediately in the active and that the noun formed from it gives us our very word metathesis, and observes that the construction which usually expresses purpose here expresses result. The imperfect passive he renders as he was still not found, and the verb of witness as a perfect passive meaning that the testimony stands on record still. On the following verse he calls the word for impossible a strong one, says that faith is a moral necessity and that this is true in business also, with banks for instance, and holds that the very existence of God is a matter of intelligent faith so that men are left without excuse. The word for rewarder he renders rather as becometh a rewarder, marking the verb as a present middle of the verb to become and not the verb to be, and notes that the compound noun is the only example in the New Testament of a late and rare double compound, found once in the papyri, formed from the words for reward and for paying back.

Cyril takes the lesson read that day as an invitation to the true faith, since it sets before the hearers the way in which they also must please God, affirming that without faith it is impossible to please him. He turns the clause immediately toward the will and toward practice, asking when a man will resolve to serve God unless he believes that he is a giver of reward, and when a young woman will choose a virgin life or a young man live soberly if they believe not that for chastity there is a crown that fadeth not away. The rewarder clause is thus for him not a speculative proposition but the ground on which any costly obedience is undertaken at all, so that the whole discipline of the Christian life rests upon a persuasion about what God will do rather than upon what can presently be seen. He closes with a figure and a proof text: faith is an eye that enlightens every conscience and imparts understanding, for the Prophet says that if you will not believe, neither shall you understand.

debates: What Enoch’s translation was: Gill excludes a spiritual translation, a rapture from place to place, and a temporary catching up such as Paul’s, insisting on a removal of soul and body to heaven as a pledge of the resurrection, while Clarke keeps only to the negative that he did not pass through death, and Ellicott and Robertson confine themselves to the vocabulary, the one preferring the bare simplicity of the Hebrew and the other tracing the verb that gives us the word metathesis

Why the manner of the removal mattered: Calvin alone asks the question and answers from the corruption of the age, that a death like other men’s would have left the providence hidden, whereas a removal without dying made the hand of God openly manifest

How the writer knows Enoch had faith when Genesis does not say so: Barnes offers either the nature of piety or a direct revelation and finds the fact implied in walking with God and in Jude’s report of his prophecy, while Ellicott derives it from the Greek rendering of that same phrase as being well pleasing to God, which the following verse then makes impossible without faith
outliers: Robertson finds the moral necessity of trust illustrated by banking, and Barnes by the relations of parent, child and spouse
Cyril grounds virginity and sobriety alike on the belief that there is an unfading crown, and calls faith an eye that enlightens every conscience
Ellicott observes that Scripture withholds the record of the translation until it has first borne witness that Enoch pleased God
Gill qualifies the impossibility by excepting the elect as considered in Christ, well pleasing to God before faith

7.pericope_label: By faith Noah, warned of things not seen as yet, prepared an ark and condemned the world

schools.summary: Gill notes first that in the Greek text Noah is called Noe, as the Septuagint interpreters of the Old Testament also call him, while Josephus calls him Noeos. The warning he renders as having received an oracle from God, in which Noah was admonished how to make an ark, as Moses was in like manner admonished how to make a tabernacle; and he observes that this oracle or warning is extant in the Genesis narrative. Calvin treats the case as a wonderful example of magnanimity. When the whole world were promising themselves impunity and securely and unrestrainedly indulging themselves in sinful pleasures, Noah alone paid regard to God’s vengeance though deferred for a considerable time; he greatly wearied himself for a hundred and twenty years in building the ark; he stood unshaken amidst the scoffs of so many ungodly men; he entertained no doubt but that he would be safe in the midst of the ruin of the whole world; and he felt sure of life as it were in the grave, even in the ark. Calvin says he will only touch briefly on the subject, since each one can better weigh all the circumstances for himself, but insists that the Apostle ascribes to faith the praise of so remarkable a fortitude. He then marks a turn in the argument: the writer has hitherto been speaking of the fathers who lived in the first age of the world, but it was a kind of regeneration when Noah and his family emerged from the deluge, and it is hence evident that in all ages men have neither been approved by God nor performed anything worthy of praise otherwise than by faith. The lesson he draws is that faith looks to the word alone and rests there when everything visible contradicts it, since Noah had nothing before his eyes for more than a century but the mockery of his neighbours and the unbroken continuance of fair weather, and yet went on building.

Clarke takes the warning as fixing the sense of an important verb: since we know from the history in Genesis that God did warn Noah, we see from this passage the real import of the verb as used in various parts of the New Testament, namely that it signifies to utter oracles, to give divine warning. On the fear he is careful to define it as being influenced by religious fear or reverence towards God, and explains why the point matters: this is mentioned to show that Noah acted not from a fear of losing his life but from the fear of God, and hence that fear is here properly attributed to faith. On the condemnation of the world he sets out the contrast in three strokes, that Noah credited God and they did not, that he walked in the way God had commanded and they did not, and that he repeatedly admonished them and they regarded it not, which aggravated their crimes while it exalted his faith and righteousness; and he quotes Dodd, that Noah’s faith and obedience condemned the world, that is the unbelievers, in the same sense in which every good man’s virtues and exhortations condemn such as will not attend to and imitate them. On the last clause he explains that Noah became entitled to that justification which is by faith, and became an heir of it in the sense that he entered into possession of what God had promised on those terms. Wesley states the whole in a sentence: Noah, being warned of things not seen as yet, that is of the future deluge, and moved with fear, prepared an ark, by which open testimony he condemned the world, who neither believed nor feared.

Barnes says it is less difficult to see that Noah must have been influenced by faith than that Abel and Enoch were, since everything which Noah did in reference to the threatened deluge was done in virtue of simple faith or belief of what God said. It was not because he could show from the course of events that things were tending to such a catastrophe, nor because such an event had occurred before rendering it probable that it would occur again, nor because this was the common belief of men and it was easy to fall into it himself; it was simply because God had informed him of it and he put unwavering reliance on the truth of the divine declaration. The word for the warning he explains as meaning divinely admonished, and the things not seen as yet as the flood which was still future, the meaning being that there were no visible signs of it and nothing which could be a basis of calculation that it would occur, since the admonition was given a hundred and twenty years before the deluge and therefore long before there could have been any natural indication. Ellicott discusses the participle rendered moved with fear, reporting that the marginal rendering being wary, or better taking forethought, is preferred by some and agrees very well with the proper meaning of the word, but judging it more probable that the writer has in view that devout godly fear which the words akin to this regularly denote in the New Testament; Noah’s obedience to the divine warning was an evidence at once of his fear of God and of the faith which gave substance and present reality to the things not seen as yet. On the connecting phrase he observes that, as in the earlier verse about Abel, the words through which are slightly ambiguous, since they may relate either to the ark or to the faith, and holds the latter reference more probable: Noah’s faith, shown in the building of the ark, exposed the unbelief of the world which would not listen to his warnings and thereby incurred the divine condemnation, our Lord using the word condemn in the same sense of the men of Nineveh and the queen of the south. By the same faith, he adds, Noah became an heir of the righteousness which is according to faith, and Noah is the first to receive that description. Robertson parses the participle of warning as a first aorist passive of the old word for oracular or divine communications, already used earlier in the epistle. The participle of fear he parses as a first aorist passive of a verb formed from an adjective compounded of the words for well and to take hold, so that it means to take hold carefully, to show oneself circumspect, to act with reverence, and notes that it occurs here only in the New Testament apart from a disputed reading in Acts, though often in the Greek Old Testament. The word for ark he glosses as shaped like a box, comparing its use for the ark of the covenant; the phrase through which he refers to Noah’s faith as shown in building; and the world he takes as sinful humanity, in the same sense as later in the chapter. On the last clause he sets the title heir of righteousness beside the description of Noah in the second epistle of Peter as a preacher of righteousness, and remarks that he himself believed his own message about the flood, adding that like Enoch he walked with God.

Chrysostom begins by observing that the Son of God, speaking of his own coming, said that in the days of Noah they married and were given in marriage, and that the Apostle therefore recalled to his readers’ minds an appropriate image. He then marks what distinguishes this instance from the preceding one: the example of Enoch was an example only of faith, whereas that of Noah is an example of unbelief also, and this is a complete consolation and exhortation, when not only are believers found approved but unbelievers suffer the opposite. On the warning he asks what being warned of God means and answers that it is having had a thing foretold to him; but he presses further and asks why the particular expression for a divine communication is used, noting that in another place it is said that a thing was communicated to Simeon by the Spirit, and again that the divine communication answered Elijah. From this he draws a doctrinal inference, that one may see here the equal dignity of the Spirit, since as God reveals so also does the Holy Spirit, the same term for an oracle serving both. The things not seen as yet he identifies concretely as the rain, which had not yet been experienced, so that Noah’s whole labour rested on a word about something of which the world had no example.

debates: What the participle rendered moved with fear means: Ellicott reports the alternative of being wary or taking forethought, which suits the proper meaning of the word, but prefers the devout godly fear which the cognates regularly carry in the New Testament, while Clarke insists on reverence toward God rather than fear for his own life and makes that the ground on which fear is here credited to faith, and Robertson derives it from taking hold carefully and renders it acting circumspectly

Whether the world was condemned through the ark or through the faith: Ellicott calls the connecting phrase ambiguous and prefers the faith, as he did in the verse about Abel, Robertson refers it to the faith as shown in building, and Wesley makes the ark itself the open testimony by which the condemnation was pronounced

Why this example is added to those before it: Chrysostom says Enoch showed faith only while Noah shows unbelief also and its punishment, which makes the passage consolation and exhortation together, and Calvin marks the emergence from the deluge as a kind of regeneration proving that no age was approved on any other terms
outliers: Chrysostom infers the equal dignity of the Spirit from the shared term for a divine oracle
Barnes stresses that the warning came a hundred and twenty years before any natural sign could appear
Calvin pictures Noah sure of life as it were in the grave, safe inside the ruin of the whole world
Clarke quotes Dodd that a good man’s virtues condemn those who will not imitate them
Gill notes the Greek form Noe and the form Noeos used by Josephus

8.pericope_label: Abraham called out, sojourning in tents, looking for the city with foundations; and Sarah’s strength to conceive

schools.summary: Gill takes the call not of Abraham’s name but of his summons out of his country, kindred and father’s house, noting the variant reading found in the Alexandrian copy and the Vulgate which would make the clause refer to his being called Abraham, and answering that though his first name Abram might be given in the faith of his being a great man and his second name Abraham when he was a believer, the change was made some years after the call referred to here. That call he treats as an emblem of the call of God’s people out from among the world. The land of promise he calls Canaan, so named because it was promised to Abraham and his seed, and typical of heaven, which is not by the works of the law but by the free promise and grace of God. On the city he is careful to exclude the nearer candidates: it is not the city of Jerusalem, nor the Gospel church state, but either the city of the new Jerusalem which is said to have twelve foundations, in which glorious state Abraham with the rest of the saints, raised from the dead, will in person possess the promised land, or else the ultimate glory of the saints in heaven where God dwells and keeps his palace, which will have in it many habitations and will be both peaceable and safe and full of glory. On Sarah he raises a question of subject: some copies add that she was barren, as the Vulgate and all the Oriental versions read, a circumstance which makes her faith appear the greater, but it is a question whether the apostle speaks of the faith of Sarah or of Abraham. Some think he speaks of Abraham’s faith and that it was through his faith that Sarah conceived, observing that the last clause may be rendered because he judged him faithful, and the rather because the apostle both before and after is speaking of Abraham’s faith. Calvin comes to Abraham as the chief father of God’s church on earth, in whose name the Jews gloried as though by the distinction of being his holy race alone they were removed from the common order of men; the writer reminds them of what they ought to possess as the main thing if they would be counted among his children, and calls their attention to faith, since Abraham himself had no excellency which did not proceed from faith. The first particular is that faith was the cause why he immediately obeyed God when commanded to remove. The second is that having entered the land he was hardly received as a stranger and a sojourner: where was the inheritance he had expected? It might instantly have occurred to his mind that he had been deceived by God, and still greater was the disappointment, which the Apostle does not mention, when shortly after a famine drove him from the country and compelled him to flee to the land of Gerar; but the Apostle considered it enough to say, as a commendation of his faith, that he became a sojourner in the land of promise. He ascribes their patience to faith because they looked forward to heaven, which was indeed to see things invisible: it was a great thing to cherish the assurance about the land until after some ages it was realised, but as they did not confine their thoughts even to that land but penetrated into heaven, it was a still clearer evidence of faith. Heaven he calls a city because of its perpetuity, for in the world there is nothing but what is transitory. On Sarah he says the example is adduced that women may know this truth belongs to them as well as to men, and is preferred to others because she was the mother of all the faithful; but it may seem strange that her faith is commended who was openly charged with unbelief, since she laughed at the word of the angel as though it were a fable, and it was not the laugh of wonder and admiration, for otherwise she would not have been so severely reproved. It must indeed be confessed that her faith was blended with unbelief. On the closing verse he prefers to render the disputed word adverbially, in the like manner, so that Abraham was like Sarah, dead as to the power of begetting children.

Henry turns the whole passage upon the reader. We are often called to leave worldly connexions, interests and comforts; if heirs of Abraham’s faith we shall obey and go forth, though not knowing what may befall us, and we shall be found in the way of duty, looking for the performance of God’s promises. The trial of Abraham’s faith was that he simply and fully obeyed the call of God. Sarah received the promise as the promise of God, and being convinced of that she truly judged that he both could and would perform it. Many who have a part in the promises do not soon receive the things promised; but faith can lay hold of blessings at a great distance, can make them present, can love them and rejoice in them though they are strangers to them, as saints whose home is heaven and as pilgrims travelling toward that home. By faith they overcome the terrors of death and bid a cheerful farewell to this world and to all the comforts and crosses of it; and those once truly and savingly called out of a sinful state have no mind to return into it. All true believers desire the heavenly inheritance, and the stronger faith is the more fervent those desires will be. Notwithstanding their meanness by nature, their vileness by sin and the poverty of their outward condition, God is not ashamed to be called the God of all true believers, such is his mercy and such his love to them; let them therefore never be ashamed of being called his people, nor of any who are truly so however much despised in the world, and above all let them take care that they are not a shame and reproach to their God.

Clarke makes the obedience the measure of the faith: since Abraham went out not knowing whither he went, his obedience was the fullest proof of his faith in God, and his faith was an implicit faith, for he obeyed and went out from his own country having no prospect of any good or success but what his implicit faith led him to expect from God as the rewarder of them that diligently seek him; and in all the preceding cases, and in all that follow, the apostle keeps this maxim fully in view. On the sojourning he remarks that it is remarkable Abraham did not acquire any right in Canaan except that of a burying place, nor did he build any house in it, his faith showing him that it was only a type and pledge of a better country, which he kept continually in view; he, with Isaac and Jacob who were heirs of the same promise, were contented to dwell in tents without any fixed habitation. On the city he says Abraham knew that earth could afford no permanent residence for an immortal mind, and looked for that heavenly building of which God is the architect and owner; in a word, he lost sight of earth that he might keep heaven in view, and all who are partakers of his faith possess the same spirit and walk by the same rule. The two closing titles he distinguishes: the first signifies an architect, one who plans, calculates and constructs a building, while the second signifies the governor or owner of what has been built. On Sarah he notes that she at first treated the divine message with ridicule, judging it to be absolutely impossible, not knowing then that it was from God, and that her age and circumstances justified this, for humanly speaking such an event was impossible; but when she knew that it was God who had spoken, it does not appear that she doubted any more, believing implicitly that what God had promised he was able to perform. On the closing verse he observes that Abraham was according to nature long past the time of the procreation of children, so that the birth of Isaac, the circumstances of the father and mother considered, was entirely supernatural, and the people who proceeded from this birth were a supernatural people, and were and are most strikingly singular through every period of their history to the present day. Wesley adds that the promise about the land had been made before, that Isaac and Jacob by the same manner of living showed the same faith, Jacob having been born fifteen years before the death of Abraham, and that as joint heirs they had all the same interest therein, Isaac not receiving the inheritance from Abraham nor Jacob from Isaac but all of them from God. On the city he remarks simply that a tent has no foundations, and that God is the sole contriver, former and finisher of the city that has them. On Sarah he notes that she laughed at first, and on the closing verse that Abraham was as it were dead until his strength was supernaturally restored, which continued for many years after.

Barnes says there is no difficulty in determining that Abraham was influenced by faith, the case being even stronger than that of Noah since it is expressly declared in Genesis that he believed in the Lord and it was counted to him for righteousness; in illustrating the power of faith the apostle appeals to two instances in which Abraham exhibited it, each requiring confidence in God of extraordinary strength. On the sojourning he says Abraham resided in Canaan as if he were a stranger, having no possessions there which he did not procure by honest purchase and owning no land in fee-simple except the small piece bought for a burial-place; in all respects he lived there as if he had no peculiar right in the soil and never expected to own it, as if he were in a country wholly owned by others, exercising no privilege of ownership. On the city he reports that it has been doubted what is referred to, that Grotius and some others suppose Jerusalem to be meant as a permanent dwelling for Abraham’s posterity in contradistinction from the unsettled life of the patriarchs, but answers that there is no evidence Abraham looked forward to the building of such a city since no promise was made to him of it, and that this interpretation falls evidently below the whole drift of the passage, which points rather to heaven. On Sarah he observes that the emphatic pronoun implies there was something remarkable in the fact that she should manifest this faith, and suspects a reference to the incredulity with which she at first received the announcement; even her strong incredulity was overcome, and though everything seemed to render the thing impossible and she was at first so disposed to laugh at the suggestion, yet her unbelief was overcome. On the closing verse he marks as worthy of remark that the whole Jewish people sprang from one man, and that as the reward of his strong faith he was made the father and founder of a nation, there being to human appearance no more probability that he would have a son at that period of life than that the dead would. Ellicott prefers the older versions which bring in the word obeyed after called, and corrects a possible misreading of the English: it may seem to imply that when called Abraham received the promise that the land to which he would be directed should be his inheritance, but it is not so, for that promise is not found in the words of the call but was bestowed when he had obeyed, and the meaning here is unto a place which he was to receive. On the sojourning he prefers, according to the true reading, a land of the promise: into a land which the promise made his own he came as a sojourner, and sojourned in it as in a land belonging to others, making his settled abode there in tents; the words he calls very expressive, especially those of the last clause, since Abraham made his home once for all, well aware that it was to be his home and expecting no change in this respect all his life long, and made it in tents, movable and shifting abodes. On the city he renders it rather the city which hath the foundations, and observes that where the strangers and pilgrims of the later verses are seeking a country of their own, here the dweller in tents is waiting for the city that hath the foundations; all these verses clearly teach that the promise as apprehended by the patriarchs was not bounded by the gift of Canaan, and though of what nature their expectations of the future life may have been we cannot tell, they knew that their fellowship with God was not to be broken. On Sarah he prefers by faith Sarah herself also, or even Sarah herself, and says this emphatic introduction of her name may point to the unbelief which for a brief while she displayed, but that the words may simply mean Sarah also on her part, the joint recipient with Abraham of a divine promise in which it might at first seem she had no part; he notes that the words rendered was delivered of a child are absent from the best authorities. Robertson parses the negative with the participle and the present indicative preserved in the indirect question, and calls Abraham a sublime and graphic example of faith who did not even know where the land was that he was going to receive as an inheritance. The verb of sojourning he traces to dwelling beside, common in the Greek Old Testament and rare in the New; the verb for looking he calls a picturesque progressive imperfect describing steady and patient waiting in spite of disappointment; and he observes that Abraham set his steady gaze on heaven as his real home, being a mere pilgrim on earth. The two closing titles he glosses as craftsman or artificer and as a worker for the people. On Sarah he renders the phrase for deposit of seed and the next as beyond the season of age, and says that even Sarah, old as she was, believed God who had promised, and hence received power. On the closing verse he parses the accusative of general reference and the perfect passive participle of a late verb meaning to make dead or treat as dead, used here by hyperbole, and renders the phrase about the shore as along the lip of the sea, noting that the adjective for innumerable occurs here alone in the New Testament.

Cyril of Jerusalem says there is much to tell of faith and that the whole day would not be time sufficient to describe it fully, so that for the present he will be content with Abraham only, as one of the examples from the Old Testament, seeing that we have been made his sons through faith. He was justified, Cyril insists, not only by works but also by faith: for though he did many things well, yet he was never called the friend of God except when he believed. Moreover his every work was performed in faith, so that faith is not one act among others in his life but the principle running through all of them. Through faith he left his parents; through faith he left country and place and home; and in like manner Cyril traces the same principle through the rest of what is recorded of him, so that the reader may see that nothing Abraham did was done on any other ground. The passage stands in Cyril as an argument to catechumens that the faith they are about to profess is not a lesser thing than works but the very root from which acceptable works grow, and that they are enrolled among Abraham’s children on that footing and no other.

debates: Whether the faith commended in the verse about Sarah is hers or Abraham’s: Gill reports the rendering because he judged him faithful and the argument from context that Abraham is the subject both before and after, while Calvin insists the example was chosen precisely so that women might know the truth belongs to them, Barnes and Ellicott both weigh the emphatic pronoun, and Ellicott allows that it may mean no more than Sarah on her part

How Sarah’s commendation squares with her laughter: Calvin concedes plainly that her faith was blended with unbelief and that the laugh was not one of wonder, since she was severely reproved for it, while Clarke argues that her age justified the incredulity so long as she did not know the message was divine and that she doubted no more once she did, and Barnes says only that her strong incredulity was overcome

What city Abraham looked for: Barnes rejects the view of Grotius and others that Jerusalem is meant, since no such promise was ever made to him and the reading falls below the drift of the passage, Gill excludes both Jerusalem and the Gospel church state in favour of the new Jerusalem or the final glory, and Ellicott argues from the whole context that the patriarchs’ expectation was never bounded by the gift of Canaan
outliers: Calvin notes the disappointment the writer passes over in silence, that a famine soon drove Abraham out of the land he had just entered
Ellicott points out that the promise of the land was given only after Abraham had obeyed, not at the call
Clarke calls the people descended from Isaac a supernatural people, singular through every period of their history
Cyril of Jerusalem observes that Abraham was never called the friend of God until he believed

13.pericope_label: These all died in faith: strangers and pilgrims seeking a better country, that is a heavenly

schools.summary: Gill takes the phrase of the believers named in the preceding verses, excepting Enoch, and particularly the three patriarchs with Sarah. These died a corporeal death, which is common to all, to the righteous and to the wicked, and yet saints die not as other men: they die in faith, having the grace itself, which being once implanted can never be lost, and sometimes in the exercise of it, as these believers did. They died in the faith of their posterity inheriting the land of Canaan, in the faith of the promised Messiah, and in the believing views of the heavenly glory. On the desire for a better country he is careful about the tense: it is not to be understood of the time at which the apostle wrote, for the patriarchs of whom he speaks were not then on earth, nor in any third place between heaven and earth, but were then in heaven; and though there are indeed in heaven desires after perfect happiness in soul and body, this passage intends the desires of these saints when on earth, which are common to all believers in the present state of things, who, as the patriarchs desired a better country than Chaldea or even Canaan itself, desire a better country than this world. Calvin enhances by a comparison the faith of the patriarchs: when they had only tasted of the promises, as though fully satisfied with their sweetness, they despised all that was in the world, and they never forgot that taste, however small it was, either in life or in death. He limits the phrase these all to Abraham and those mentioned after him, since to them the promises had been made and of them only the writer speaks, following Beza and Stuart, and reports that the expression is differently explained, some understanding simply that they died in faith because in this life they never enjoyed the promised blessings. On the possibility of return he says the writer anticipates an objection that might have been made, that they were strangers because they had left their own country; the apostle meets this and says that though they called themselves strangers they yet did not think of Mesopotamia, for if they had a desire to return they might have done so, but they had willingly banished themselves from it, nay had disowned it as though it did not belong to them, so that by another country they meant that which is beyond this world. On the last verse he refers to the words spoken at the bush, that God is the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob, and calls it a singular honour when God makes men illustrious by attaching his name to them, designing thus to have himself distinguished from idols; this privilege also depends on faith, for when the holy fathers aspired to a celestial country God on the other hand counted them as citizens. We are hence to conclude, he says, that there is no place for us among God’s children except we renounce the world, and that there will be for us no inheritance in heaven except we become pilgrims on the earth.

Clarke takes the phrase of Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Jacob, who continued to believe to the end of their lives that God would fulfil the promise, though they neither saw the numerous seed nor obtained the promised rest in Canaan. The two words he defines with care: strangers are persons who are out of their own country and in a foreign land, while pilgrims are sojourners only for a time, not intending to take up their abode in that place nor to get naturalised in that country; and he turns the definition into a rebuke, asking how many use these expressions and profess to be strangers and pilgrims here below while the whole of their conduct contradicts it.
