On the confession he says that a man’s country is that in which he has constitutional rights and privileges, and that no stranger or sojourner has any such rights where he sojourns; these, by declaring that they felt themselves strangers and sojourners, professed their faith in a heavenly country and state and looked beyond the grave for a place of happiness, since no intelligent Jew could suppose that Canaan was all the rest which God had promised to his people. On the possibility of return he explains why they never took it: they considered their right to the promises of God as dependent on their utter renunciation of Chaldea, and it was this that induced Abraham to make his steward Eliezer swear that he would not carry his son Isaac back to Chaldea, where idolatry reigned, God having called them to be the progenitors of a people among whom the knowledge of the true God should be established and preserved. On the last verse he says they all expected spiritual blessings and a heavenly inheritance, sought God as their portion, and did so in such a way and on such principles that he is not ashamed to be called their God, showing his affection by preparing for them a city, namely heaven, as they themselves would seek no city on earth; and from this it is evident, he adds, that the patriarchs had a proper notion of the immortality of the soul and expected a place of residence widely different from Canaan. Wesley says that in death faith acts most vigorously, glosses the promises as the promised blessings, and explains the embracing as what one does to a dear friend when he meets him. Of the return he says only that had they been mindful of their earthly country, Ur of the Chaldeans, they might easily have returned; and of the last verse, that it is a full convincing proof that the patriarchs had a revelation and a promise of eternal glory in heaven, so that God is not ashamed to be called their God, seeing he has prepared for them a city worthy of God to give.

Barnes restricts the phrase to those just mentioned, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Sarah, arguing that although it was true of Abel and Noah also that they died in faith they are not included in this declaration, since the promises were not particularly entrusted to them, and that if the word these were made to include them it must include Enoch also, who did not die at all. The phrase itself, he insists, does not mean that they died in the exercise or possession of religion but more strictly that they died not having possessed what was the object of their faith, having been looking for something future. On the confession he draws a comparison from ordinary observation: we should think in the same way of any strange people coming among us now who lived in tents, who frequently changed their residence, who became the purchasers of no land except to bury their dead, and who never spoke of becoming permanent residents; we should think that they were in search of some place as their home and that they had not yet found it, and such people were the Hebrew patriarchs. On the possibility of return he says that if they had remembered their old country with sufficient interest and affection to make them desirous of returning, they might have had opportunity, the journey being neither so long nor so perilous that they could not have retraced their steps, since it would have been no more difficult or dangerous than the first journey; this shows that their remaining as strangers and sojourners in the land of Canaan was voluntary, and that they preferred it with all its inconveniences and hardships to a return to their native land. On the last verse he says that at the time referred to, when they confessed themselves strangers and sojourners, they showed that they sought a better country than the one they had left, living as if they had no expectation of a permanent residence on earth and were looking to another world; the argument appears to be based on what is apparent from the whole history, that they had a confident belief that the land of Canaan would be given to their posterity while for themselves they had no expectation of permanently dwelling there. Ellicott warns that we must not change the order of the original: seven verses up to this point have begun with the emphatic words by faith, and there is a change here though not in the emphasis of the thought, for we should not expect to read by faith these died, and what is said is that in accordance with faith all these died, faith having been the support and guide of their life so that their death was in accordance with the same principle. On the confession he cites the very words, Abraham’s declaration at Machpelah that he was a stranger and a sojourner, and Jacob’s answer to Pharaoh about the days of the years of his pilgrimage and the pilgrimage of his fathers, and renders the clause better as making it plain that they are seeking a home or fatherland. On the possibility of return he prefers they would have had opportunity to return, since all their life long they would have been able to claim again their earlier fatherland by returning whence they came. On the last verse he traces the movement of the whole passage: they confess themselves but sojourners and thus make it plain that they are still seeking their true home, and yet if they had sought nothing more than an earthly home there is one already which was once theirs and to which they might return, hence it is no earthly but a heavenly country that they desire; and he notes the close analogy this presents to the earlier argument of the epistle about the rest, where likewise words which might appear to have but an earthly reference are seen to have a higher and spiritual import. Robertson marks the break in the routine formula and renders the phrase according to faith, either for literary variety or, as Moffatt suggests, to present faith as the sphere and standard of their characters. He takes these all of the persons in the preceding verses, parses the participle of obtaining as a first aorist middle, and raises the difficulty that the author elsewhere mentions Abraham as having obtained the promise, answering that he received the promise of the Messiah but did not live to see the Messiah come as we have done. The noun for country he glosses as the land of the fathers, one’s native land, comparing our own words patriotic and patriotism. On the possibility of return he parses a condition of the second class with the imperfect in both halves rather than the aorist, so that the sense is that had they continued mindful they would have kept on having the opportunity, and remarks that continual hankering would have found a way, comparing the Israelites in the wilderness yearning after Egypt. On the last verse he parses the verb as a present middle of an old word for stretching out after or yearning after, and notes the predicate nominative with the epexegetic infinitive.

Chrysostom takes the confession of the patriarchs as the foundation of the whole Christian ethic. The first virtue, indeed the whole of virtue, is to be a stranger to this world and a sojourner, and to have nothing in common with the things here but to hang loose from them as from things strange to us. He points forward in the chapter to those blessed men of whom it is said that they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted and tormented, and of whom the world was not worthy, and observes that they called themselves strangers on that ground. But he will not let the readers rest even there, for Paul said something much beyond this: he did not merely call himself a stranger but said that he was dead to the world and that the world was dead to him, which Chrysostom takes as the further stage of the same disposition, since a stranger still has dealings with the country he passes through while a dead man has none at all. The practical force he draws out is that to be a sojourner is not a misfortune to be endured but the very form of the virtue commended in these examples, so that the readers, who were tempted to grasp again at the security they had lost, should reckon their homelessness the mark of their calling rather than a sign that God had failed them.

debates: Who is included in these all: Barnes excludes Abel and Noah because the promises were not entrusted to them, and points out that including them would draw in Enoch, who never died at all, while Calvin restricts the phrase the same way on Beza’s and Stuart’s authority

Whether Abraham did after all obtain the promise: Robertson raises the difficulty from the earlier chapter and answers that he received the promise of the Messiah without living to see him come, while Barnes distinguishes dying in the possession of religion from dying without possession of what faith was set upon

Why the formula of the chapter changes at this verse: Ellicott insists that the order of the original must stand, so that the sense is not that these died by faith but that their dying was in accordance with faith, and Robertson allows either literary variety or, with Moffatt, faith as the sphere and standard of their characters
outliers: Chrysostom takes being a stranger to the world as the whole of virtue, and points beyond it to Paul, who called himself not a stranger but a dead man
Robertson notes that continual hankering would have found a way back, as the Israelites hankered after Egypt
Clarke traces Abraham’s oath binding Eliezer not to take Isaac to Chaldea back to this renunciation
Calvin makes the divine title at the burning bush a citizenship conferred in exchange for the pilgrimage accepted

17.pericope_label: By faith Abraham offered up Isaac: command against promise, and a son received back in a figure

schools.summary: Gill takes the trial as a temptation by God, respecting the command to offer up Isaac, and answers the moral objection at once: this lays no foundation for a charge against God either of sin or of cruelty, for God’s will is the rule of justice and goodness and whatever he requires is just and good; and though his creatures are bound by the laws he prescribes them, he himself is not. Besides, he is the Lord of life, the giver and preserver of it, and he has a right to dispose of it and to take it away when, and by what means and instruments, he thinks fit; to which may be added that the secret will of God was not that Isaac should die, but a command was given to Abraham to offer him up for the trial of his faith. On the words that follow he prefers, with the Vulgate Latin and Syriac versions, the rendering to whom it was said, referring the clause to Abraham rather than to Isaac, since it was to Abraham that the promise about the seed had been spoken. On the reasoning he is careful about what exactly was concluded: Abraham did not go about this affair without thought, and yet he did not consult with flesh and blood, for his reasoning was the reasoning of faith, and the conclusion of it was not that he believed God would raise his son from the dead but that he was able to do so. He knew that he had received him at first as it were from the dead, since he sprang from his own dead body and out of Sarah’s dead womb; and though his faith did not prescribe to God, yet as he believed the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead he might believe that God would raise his son rather than that his promise should fail, this conclusion proceeding upon the power and faithfulness of God. Calvin proceeds with the history and relates the offering up of the son as a singular instance of firmness, so that there is hardly another like it to be found; hence, for the sake of enhancing it, the writer adds that Abraham was tried. Abraham had indeed already proved what he was by many trials, yet as this trial surpassed every other the Apostle would have it regarded above all his trials, as though he had said that the highest excellency of Abraham was the sacrificing of his son, for God is said to have then in an especial manner tried him. And yet this act flowed from faith, so that Abraham had nothing more excellent than faith, which brought forth such extraordinary fruit; the word rendered tried, he adds, means no other thing than proved. On the last clause he says that hope did not disappoint Abraham, for it was a sort of resurrection when his son was so suddenly delivered from the midst of death. The word there used is variously explained, and Calvin takes it simply as meaning likeness, for though Isaac did not really rise from the dead he yet seemed to have in a manner risen when he was suddenly and wonderfully rescued through the unexpected favour of God; the meaning given by Stuart and some others he calls very far fetched, though said to be natural, namely that Abraham believed God could raise Isaac from the dead because he had as it were already obtained him from the dead, being born of those who were dead as to these things.

Clarke fills in what was actually done, saying that Abraham did in effect offer up Isaac: he built an altar, bound his son, laid him upon the altar, had ready the incense, took the knife, and would immediately have slain him had he not been prevented by the same authority by which the sacrifice was enjoined. Isaac is here called his only-begotten, Clarke explains, as he was the only son Abraham had by his legitimate wife, who was heir to his property and heir of the promises of God; and the man who proved faithful in such a trial deserved to have his faith and obedience recorded throughout the world. On the reasoning he says Abraham staggered not at the promise through unbelief but was strong in faith, giving glory to God, and draws a wider inference: the resurrection of the dead must have been a doctrine of the patriarchs, for they expected a heavenly inheritance, they saw that they died as other men did, and they must have known that they could not enjoy that inheritance except in consequence of a resurrection from the dead. On the closing phrase he offers a distinctive rendering, referring to his own discourse on parabolical writing, that the word can sometimes mean a daring exploit or a jeoparding of the life, and thinks it should be so understood here as pointing out the imminent danger in which Isaac stood of losing his life. Wesley calls the occasion a glorious trial, and says of the offering that the will was accepted as if Abraham had actually done the deed. He notes that the promises received included particularly the grand promise that in Isaac should his seed be called, and that the son offered was this very son, the only one he had by Sarah, from whom the blessed seed should spring. On the reasoning he observes that Abraham accounted God able even to raise him from the dead though there had not been any instance of this in the world, and on the last clause that the receiving back is to speak in a figurative way, since Abraham did receive him afterwards, snatched from the jaws of death.

Barnes says the apostle has already stated one strong instance of Abraham’s faith and now refers to one still more remarkable, undoubtedly the strongest illustration of faith ever evinced in our world. The word rendered tried he traces through its other renderings in the New Testament, tempted in the Gospels and in many other places, prove, hath gone about, examine and tried, and insists that it does not mean here, as it often does, to place inducements before a man to lead him to do wrong, but to subject his faith to a trial in order to test its genuineness and strength, so that Abraham was placed in circumstances which showed what was in him. On the promise he notes that a numerous posterity had been promised and that it was expressly said this promise was not to be fulfilled through the son of the bondwoman Hagar but through Isaac; of course it was implied that Isaac was to reach manhood, and yet notwithstanding this, and notwithstanding that Abraham fully believed it, he prepared deliberately in obedience to the divine command to put him to death. The phrase about the seed being called he explains as meaning that Abraham’s posterity was to be named after Isaac or to descend only from him, the word called in the Scriptures being often equivalent to the verb to be. On the reasoning he holds that Abraham believed not only that God was able to raise him but that he would, since this idea is plainly implied in the whole narrative: there was no other way in which the promise could be fulfilled, and Abraham reasoned justly, having received the promise of a numerous posterity, having been told expressly that it was to be through this favourite child, being now commanded to put him to death as a sacrifice, and preparing to do it; to fulfil the promises therefore there was no other way possible but for the child to be raised from the dead, and the child had in any case been given to him at first in a supernatural manner. Ellicott observes that the patriarchs displayed their faith in the attitude of their whole life and in their death, which has been the thought of the preceding verses, and that the writer now passes to the lessons taught by particular actions and events. On the tense he notes that the Greek says hath offered up Isaac, and that several other examples of a similar peculiarity will present themselves in this chapter: as in former cases the reference is to the permanent record of Scripture in which the fact related is ever present, so that Abraham stands before us there as having offered his son, and the offering is spoken of as if consummated, since as regards faith the sacrifice was indeed complete. On the following words he says the relative means Isaac, but that the Greek words should perhaps be rendered to whom, that is to Abraham, even he to whom it was said. On the reasoning he prefers to take the words as the expression of a general truth, accounting that God is able to raise up even from the dead, and says that the faith which tests and brings conviction of the things not seen made this reasoning possible and gave power to act upon it even when Isaac must be slain; the last clause he renders from whence he did in a figure, literally in a parable, receive him, so that as in a figure the offering was completely carried out, in figure also he received his son back from the dead. Robertson parses the participle of trial as a present passive, the test being still going on, and the verb of offering as a perfect active of the verb so often used in this epistle, the act being already consummated so far as Abraham was concerned when it was interrupted, and standing on record about him; the verb that follows he parses as an imperfect of an interrupted action, comparing the naming of John the Baptist. The participle for receiving the promises he traces to an old verb meaning to welcome or entertain, rare in the New Testament, and remarks that it seemed the death of his hopes. On the following words he parses the first aorist passive and observes that God’s very words were in the heart of Abraham now about his only son. On the reasoning he parses the aorist middle participle and states the difficulty plainly: Abraham had God’s clear command that contravened God’s previous promise, and this was his solution of his difficult situation, since God had given him Isaac in his old age and God can raise him from the dead, while it was Abraham’s duty to obey God. Because of Abraham’s superb faith, he concludes, Isaac was spared and so he received him back as almost from the dead, and this is the test that Abraham stood of which James speaks.

Chrysostom marks what makes this trial different in kind from all that have gone before. Great indeed was the faith of Abraham, for while in the case of Abel and of Noah and of Enoch there was an opposition of reasonings only, so that it was necessary to go beyond human reasonings, in this case it was necessary not only to go beyond human reasonings but to manifest something more besides. For what was of God seemed to be opposed to what was of God, and faith opposed faith, and command promise. He sets out the collision in the very words of the narrative: God had said, Get thee out of thy country and from thy kindred, and I will give thee this land, and yet, as the martyr Stephen observed, he gave him no inheritance in it, not so much as to set his foot on, so that what was done was opposed to the promise. Again God had said that in Isaac shall thy seed be called, and then commanded that this same Isaac be offered up, so that the second word appeared to cancel the first. The force of the example for Chrysostom lies exactly here, that Abraham was not asked merely to believe what reason could not reach but to hold two divine words together when they seemed to destroy each other, and to obey the later without letting go the earlier. That, he urges, is what the readers are called to in their own affliction, where the promises they have received seem contradicted by what God is presently permitting to befall them.

debates: What the word rendered tried means: Barnes traces it through its renderings elsewhere and insists it does not here mean the placing of inducements to do wrong but the testing of faith for genuineness and strength, while Calvin says simply that it means proved and Gill answers the moral objection that God could not righteously command such a thing

Whether the relative in the following verse refers to Isaac or to Abraham: Gill prefers to whom it was said on the authority of the Vulgate and Syriac, Ellicott allows that the Greek means Isaac but thinks the rendering to whom perhaps right, and Robertson keeps the passive and locates the words in Abraham’s heart

What Abraham actually concluded: Barnes holds that he believed God not only could but would raise Isaac, since no other way of fulfilling the promise remained, while Gill restricts the conclusion to God’s ability and denies that faith prescribed to God, and Ellicott generalises the clause into a statement that God is able to raise up even from the dead

What receiving him in a figure means: Calvin takes the word as likeness, Isaac having seemed in a manner to rise when he was rescued, and rejects Stuart’s reading as far fetched, Ellicott makes the figure answer to the figurative completeness of the offering, and Clarke proposes that the word can denote a daring exploit or a jeoparding of the life
outliers: Chrysostom sets command against promise and faith against faith, and cites Stephen that Abraham was given not so much as a foot of the land
Robertson notes the shift from perfect to imperfect as marking an act consummated and then interrupted
Clarke infers the patriarchs’ belief in the resurrection from their expectation of a heavenly inheritance
Wesley observes that no instance of a resurrection had yet occurred in the world

20.pericope_label: Isaac blessing his sons, Jacob worshipping on his staff, and Joseph giving commandment concerning his bones

schools.summary: Gill notes that of Isaac’s two sons the former was a good man and, though the youngest, is set before the other and was blessed before him, while the latter was a wicked man and yet had a blessing, for temporal blessings are enjoyed in common; and the blessing was prophetic, concerning things to come. Jacob’s portion he takes as plenty of temporal things, under which may be signified the dews of divine grace, the fatness of God’s house, the bread of life and the wine of divine love which true Israelites partake of, together with dominion over his brother and government over nations, which had their accomplishment in his posterity. Of the second instance he observes that a dying hour was the usual time of blessing with the patriarchs, and the reason for it was that what was said might be the more attended to and regarded and more strongly impressed upon the mind; this is itself a proof that the act was done in faith, since there was then no appearance of the fulfilment of these things and no likelihood that Jacob should see it. That he blessed the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, under the direction and inspiration of the Spirit of God appears, Gill says, from his setting Ephraim before Manasseh. Of Joseph he says that his riches and honours, as they could not secure him from death, so they did not make him unmindful of it, nor was he afraid of dying or uneasy about it; nor did his prosperity make him proud or above speaking to his brethren, nor revengeful toward them, nor unmindful of their future afflictions; nor did his affluence of temporal things take off his regard to the divine promises or weaken his faith in them. Calvin explains what makes a blessing an act of faith: it was the work of faith to bless as to future things, for when the thing itself does not exist and the word only appears, faith must necessarily bear rule. He distinguishes the sense: to bless often means to pray for a blessing, but Isaac’s blessing was very different, being as it were an introduction into the possession of the land which God had promised to him and his posterity, and yet he had nothing in that land but the right of burial, so that the titles he pronounced, that peoples should serve and tribes bow down, seemed strange from one who was himself hardly a free man. On the blessing of Joseph’s sons he says it was the Apostle’s object to attribute to faith whatever was worthy of remembrance in the history of the people, and that since it would have been tedious to recount everything he selected a few things out of many; the tribe of Ephraim was so superior to the rest that they in a manner lay down under its shade, Scripture often including the ten tribes under that name. Yet Ephraim was the younger of the two sons of Joseph, and when Jacob blessed him and his brother both were young. What did Jacob observe in the younger to prefer him to the firstborn? Nay, when he did so, his eyes were dim with age so that he could not see, nor did he lay his right hand by chance on the head of Ephraim but crossed his hands deliberately. On Joseph’s dying charge Calvin says this is the last thing Moses records of the patriarchs and deserves to be particularly noticed, for wealth, luxuries and honours did not make the holy man forget the promise nor detain him in Egypt, which was evidence of no small faith; whence had he so much greatness of mind as to look down on whatever was elevated in the world, except that he had ascended up into heaven? In ordering his bones to be exported he had no regard to himself, as though his grave in the land of Canaan would be sweeter or better than in Egypt, but his only object was to sharpen the desire of his own nation, that they might more earnestly aspire after redemption.

Henry treats the three deathbed scenes together and draws the practical lesson from them. Things present are not the best things, and no man knows love or hatred by having them or wanting them. Jacob lived by faith, and he died by faith and in faith; and though the grace of faith is of use always through our whole lives, it is especially so when we come to die, for faith has a great work to do at last, to help the believer to die to the Lord so as to honour him by patience, hope and joy. Of Joseph he observes that he was tried by temptations to sin, by persecution for keeping his integrity, and also by honours and power in the court of Pharaoh, yet his faith carried him through all three, which Henry treats as the harder testimony, since prosperity is a trial as real as affliction and one that fewer survive. He adds the reflection that it is a great mercy to be free from wicked laws and edicts, but that when we are not so we must use all lawful means for our own preservation and the preservation of those entrusted to us, as the parents of Moses did in their own time; and throughout he keeps the emphasis on faith acting at the close of life, when nothing remains to be seen and everything must be taken on the word of God alone.

Clarke says of the first instance that Isaac believed God would fulfil his promise to his posterity, and that God gave him to see what would befall them in their future generations; he then enters a caution about the use afterwards made of the passage, that the apostle does not seem to intimate that one son should be an object of divine hatred and the other of divine love in reference to their eternal states, this being wholly a discovery of later ages. On the second instance he reconstructs the scene at length. At the time Joseph visited his father, Jacob was very weak and generally confined to his couch, having at hand his staff, either that with which he usually supported his feeble body or that which was the ensign of his office as patriarch or chief of a very numerous family; and the ancient chiefs in all countries had this staff or sceptre continually at hand, as may be seen throughout Homer. He recalls that when Joseph came to see his father in his last sickness Israel strengthened himself and sat upon the bed, so that the posture described is entirely natural. On the third instance he notes that the verb means when he was dying, and that the charge was given concerning his bones; and he adds a conjecture of his own about the sarcophagus now in the British Museum, vulgarly called Alexander’s coffin, that it is more probably the coffin of Joseph himself, and that should the time ever arrive when the hieroglyphics upon it are interpreted, this conjecture may appear to have had its foundation in truth. Wesley says of the first that Isaac prophetically foretold the particular blessings his sons should partake of, preferring the elder before the younger in the order of naming; of the second, that Jacob was near death and bowed down on the top of his staff as he sat on the side of his bed; and of the third, that the charge concerning the bones was that they should be carried into the land of promise.

Barnes explains the first instance as meaning that Isaac pronounced a blessing on his sons in respect to their future condition, and that this was by faith in God who had communicated it to him and in full confidence that he would accomplish all that was predicted; the act of faith here was simply that which believes all that God says is true. There were no human probabilities at the time when these prophetic announcements were made which could have been the basis of his calculation, so that all he said must have rested merely on the belief that God had revealed it to him; and a blessing was pronounced on each of a very different nature, yet Isaac had no doubt that both would be fulfilled. On the second instance he sets out the textual question fully: the words are an exact quotation from the Greek version, while the English version of the Genesis passage has Israel bowing himself upon the bed’s head, which is in the main a proper translation of the Hebrew word; that word, however, with different points means a branch, a bough, a rod or a staff, and the translators of the Greek version have so rendered it. The Masoretic points, Barnes insists, are of no authority, and either translation is therefore proper. On the third instance he explains that the prediction of the departure could have rested only on faith in the promise of God, there being no events then occurring likely to lead to it and nothing which could serve as a basis of calculation except what God had spoken; the faith of Joseph was therefore simple confidence in God, and its strength was seen in his firm conviction that what God had promised would come to pass. Ellicott judges it probable, though not certain, that the word even should be inserted before the closing phrase of the first instance, so that the emphasis rests there: Isaac had regard not to things present only, or things almost at hand, but looked far into the future through the divine revelation which opened to him the meaning of the promises received by Abraham, and so gave to each son the blessing designed by God. In the second instance he prefers each of the sons to both, since the separate character of the two blessings is thus brought out, and he observes that the order of time is reversed in this verse, probably so that the blessing of Jacob may immediately follow the similar record of the verse before. On the worship he refers to the scene in Genesis where, after receiving from Joseph a promise confirmed by oath that he should be buried with his fathers, Israel bowed himself upon, or worshipped towards, the bed’s head; in the Greek version and in the Targums the words are understood as denoting an act of worship, and the Greek translators have taken the last word of the Hebrew verse to denote a staff. On the third instance he renders the opening literally as drawing to his end, notes that the word is taken from the close of Genesis and that the mention of the departure is literally the Exodus, and says this example of faith in the promise and clinging to the hope it held forth needs no comment; for the fulfilment of the dying request he points to Moses taking the bones of Joseph with him out of Egypt and to their burial at Shechem. Robertson notes only that the first instance is as told in the Genesis narrative of the blessing of Jacob and Esau. On the second he observes that the phrase comes from the Greek version but that there is no word for leaning in it at all, the Hebrew having the head of the bed, and that the Hebrew word allows either meaning with different vowel points. On the third he parses the opening participle as a present active meaning finishing his life, glosses the noun for the departure as a late compound for a way out or exit used metaphorically of death, and notes the uncontracted form of the word for bones.

Chrysostom takes the phrase about things to come as raising a large question. Our Lord said that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things his hearers saw and did not see them, and to hear what they heard and did not hear it; did then those righteous men know all the things to come? Chrysostom answers, yea, most certainly. His reasoning is that if the Son was not revealed because of the weakness of those who were not able to receive him, he was with good reason revealed to those conspicuous in virtue, so that the very argument which explains the concealment establishes the disclosure in their case; and this, he says, is what Paul means by saying that they knew the things to come, namely the resurrection of Christ. He is careful, however, to leave the alternative open: or the writer does not mean this, but that the phrase concerning things to come refers not to the world to come but to things still future in this world, so that Isaac’s blessing looked forward to what would befall his sons’ posterity within history. Either way the point Chrysostom presses is the same, that the patriarchs were not men groping in the dark but men to whom God had genuinely shown what was ahead, and who acted on what they had been shown.

debates: Whether Jacob worshipped leaning on his staff or bowed on the bed’s head: Barnes sets out that the same Hebrew consonants with different points give either sense, declares the Masoretic points of no authority and allows both renderings, Robertson notes that the original has no word for leaning at all, Ellicott reports that the Greek version and the Targums alike read the act as worship and took the last word for a staff, while Clarke reconstructs a scene in which the staff was at hand either as a support or as the ensign of office, and Wesley keeps him seated on the side of the bed

Whether the righteous of old knew what was to come: Chrysostom answers most certainly, arguing that the Son was hidden only from the weak and therefore revealed to those conspicuous in virtue, but allows the alternative that things to come may mean things still future within this world rather than the world to come

How far the blessing of Jacob and Esau bears on their eternal states: Clarke enters an express caution that the apostle does not intimate one to be an object of divine hatred and the other of divine love in that respect, calling this wholly a discovery of later ages, while Gill notes that the wicked son had a blessing too, since temporal blessings are enjoyed in common
outliers: Calvin observes that Jacob’s eyes were dim with age, so that the crossing of his hands over Ephraim cannot have been his own choosing
Clarke appeals to Homer for the chief’s staff kept continually at hand, and guesses that the sarcophagus called Alexander’s coffin may be Joseph’s
Calvin says Joseph ordered his bones out of Egypt not for his own sake but to sharpen his nation’s desire for redemption
Ellicott points out that the two events of the middle verse are given in reverse chronological order

23.pericope_label: Moses hidden by his parents, refusing to be called Pharaoh’s daughter’s son, and esteeming the reproach of Christ

schools.summary: Gill is careful at the outset that the faith here spoken of is not that of Moses but of his parents at the time of his birth, which was when Pharaoh had published an edict ordering every male child to be cast into the river; instead of obeying that order they hid him three months in his father’s house, as the Ethiopic version expressly says. He reports the Targumist’s tradition that his mother went with him but six months, at the end of which he was born, and that she hid him three months, which made up the nine in which a woman usually goes with child. On the refusal he glosses the expression as meaning that Moses was great, a nobleman in Pharaoh’s court, or that he had arrived at great knowledge, being learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, or rather that he was well advanced in years, being full forty years of age. On the choice he says the people Moses joined were the Israelites, God’s chosen and peculiar people and the true worshippers of him, and that the company and conversation of such is most eligible to every good man because God is with them, his word and ordinances are with them, and there are large provisions of grace in the midst of them, so that it is profitable and delightful and honourable to be among them; but then they are a poor and an afflicted people, affliction being with them for the sake of God and of Christ. On the reproach he allows two senses: either Christ personal, meaning not any reproach that lay upon Christ as the immediate object of it but reproach borne for his sake, since Christ was made known to the Old Testament saints who believed in him and was typified by the sacrifices they offered, so that they were reproached for the sacrifices and the worship and their expectation of the Messiah; or Christ mystical, that is the church, so called because of its union to him. Calvin distinguishes the motive of Moses’ parents from a merely natural one: there have been others, and those heathens, who from no fear of God but only from a desire of propagating an offspring preserved their own children at the peril of life, but the Apostle shows that the parents of Moses were induced to save him for another reason, namely that as God had promised them under their oppression that a deliverer would come at some time, they relied confidently on that promise and preferred the safety of the infant to their own. He grants the difficulty that the writer seems to say what is contrary to the character of faith when he grounds the act on the beauty of the child. On the refusal he says the example of Moses ought to have been remembered by the Jews more than that of any other, for through him they were delivered from bondage, the covenant of God was renewed with them, and the constitution of the Church was established by the publication of the Law; but if faith is to be considered as the main thing in Moses, it would be very strange and unreasonable that he should draw them away to anything else, whence it follows that all they make a poor proficiency in the Law who are not guided by it to faith. On the pleasures of sin he draws a practical rule: this clause ought to be carefully noticed, for we here learn that we ought to shun as a deadly poison whatever cannot be enjoyed without offending God, since by that name he calls all the allurements of the world which draw us away from God and our calling; but the comforts of our earthly life which we are allowed by pure conscience and God’s permission to enjoy are not included here, so that we ought ever to remember to know and understand what God allows us, some things being in themselves lawful whose use is nevertheless prohibited to us owing to circumstances of time or place.

Clarke fills in what Moses surrendered. We know that he was bred up at the Egyptian court and was there considered to be the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, and probably might have succeeded to the throne of Egypt; but finding that God had visited his people and given them a promise of spiritual and eternal blessings, he chose rather to take the lot of this people, that is God as his portion for ever, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin, which however gratifying to the animal senses could only be temporary. He notes in passing that after the verse about the hiding of the child a whole clause is added by certain manuscripts and versions, and considers what weight it should carry. On the reproach of Christ he explains that the Christ or Messiah had been revealed to Moses, of whom he prophesied that God would raise up a prophet like himself, and that the reproach which God’s people had in consequence of their decided opposition to idolatry may be termed the reproach of Christ, since they refused to become one people with the Egyptians because the promise of the rest was made to them, and in this rest Christ and his salvation were included. He grants that it does not appear these things were known to the Hebrews at large, but holds it evident that sufficient intimations were given to Moses concerning the great Deliverer, of whom Moses himself was a type. Wesley says of the parents that they saw doubtless with a divine presage of things to come, and of the reproach that it was what Moses bore for believing in the Messiah to come and acting accordingly. On the recompense he is exact: Moses looked off from all those perishing treasures and beyond all those temporal hardships unto the recompence of reward, and that reward was not an inheritance in Canaan, for he had no warrant from God to look for this, nor did he ever attain it, but what his believing ancestors looked for, a future state of happiness in heaven.

Barnes states that the faith commended at the birth is that of the parents, the faith of Moses himself being commended in the following verses; they were led to preserve his life by their confidence in God, believing that he was destined to some great purpose and would be spared notwithstanding all the probabilities against it. He notes that Exodus says the hiding was done by his mother, and that the truth doubtless was that the mother was the agent, since the concealment of an infant would naturally devolve on her, though the apostle speaks of both parents as consenting. On the refusal he observes that the Greek is being great, that is grown up to manhood, and that Moses was at that time forty years of age, so that he took this step in the full maturity of his judgment and when there was no danger of being influenced by the ardent passions of youth. On the choice he sets out both halves of the calculation: the people of God were then oppressed and downtrodden, poor and crushed and despised, a nation of slaves, so that if Moses cast in his lot with them his condition would be one of great trial, while if he sought to elevate and deliver them the undertaking could not but be one of great peril and hardship. On the reproach of Christ he offers three possible meanings: that Moses was willing to bear the reproaches incident to his belief that the Messiah would come, and gave up his fair prospects in Egypt with that expectation; or that he endured such reproaches as Christ suffered; or that the apostle uses the expression as a sort of technical phrase, well understood in his time, to denote sufferings endured in the cause of religion, since Christians would naturally describe all sufferings on account of religion as endured in the cause of Christ. Ellicott explains that the word rendered proper has its now obsolete sense of handsome or comely, a meaning not uncommon in Shakespeare, and that the word used in the Greek translation of Exodus is preserved both in Stephen’s speech and here; it would seem, he says, that the remarkable beauty of the infant was understood by his parents as a divine sign given for the guidance of their conduct, and the next clause should probably be closely connected with this, since their reliance on the protection of God enabled them to brave the anger of the king. On the refusal he notes that the words are taken from the Greek translation of the passage where we first read of Moses as openly associating himself with his oppressed people: when he slew the Egyptian who was smiting a Hebrew, one of his brethren, he in act refused to be called a son of Pharaoh’s daughter and chose to suffer affliction with the people of God. On the choice he prefers having chosen, since the act was an expression of a deliberate choice, and observes that Moses joined his people because it was the people of God, so that to stand aloof for the sake of ease and pleasure would for him have been apostasy from God, which is why the alternative is called sin; the faith of Moses had brought conviction of the things not seen, which are eternal, and hence he looked not at the things seen which are for a season. On the reproach he insists on the reproach of the Christ, and rejects as impossible several proposed explanations, among them reproach for Christ and reproach similar to that which Christ endured; the first point to be noted, he says, is that the words are almost exactly a quotation from one of the chief of the Messianic psalms, where the enemies of the Lord are said to have reproached the footsteps of his Anointed. Robertson parses the passive verb of hiding and the old adjective used as a neuter substantive for extent of time, and renders the description of the child literally as the child was goodly, tracing the adjective to the word for a city so that it means of the city, citified, of polished manners, genteel, and noting that it occurs in the New Testament only here and in Stephen’s speech, about Moses both times; the word for the king’s commandment he calls a late compound occurring only here. On the refusal he renders the participle having become great, parses the verb of refusal as a first aorist middle, and remarks that Moses was of age and made his choice not from ignorance. On the choice he renders the participle rather having chosen, parses the double compound infinitive meaning to be ill treated along with others, and notes that it is known only here and in one papyrus of the second century, though the simple verb occurs later in the epistle; the other phrase he renders literally as to have temporary pleasure of sin. On the reproach he cites the same Messianic psalm, holds that the Anointed One is what is meant and is here rightly applied by the writer to Jesus as the Messiah who had his own shame to bear, and adds that there is today as then a special reproach in being a follower of Jesus Christ; Moses took this obloquy as greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, and was laying up treasure in heaven.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses this verse in an argument about who it was that appeared to Moses. That you may be sure that this is he who was seen of Moses, he says, hear Paul’s testimony, when he says that they all drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and that the rock was Christ; and again, that by faith Moses forsook Egypt, and shortly after, that he accounted the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt. From these two statements set side by side Cyril concludes that the Christ was present in the events of the exodus and was the object of Moses’ faith, so that the reproach borne was borne for a person then known and not merely for a doctrine afterwards revealed. He then presses the point through the request Moses made, when he said to him, Shew me thyself, that I may see thee with understanding; and he draws the inference that the prophets also in those times saw the Christ, that is, as far as each was able. The limit is as important to him as the vision: the answer given was that there shall no man see my face and live, so that what was granted to Moses was a real but partial sight, suited to what a man in this life can bear.

debates: What the reproach of Christ means: Ellicott insists on the reproach of the Christ and rejects both reproach for Christ and reproach like Christ’s as impossible, deriving the phrase from a Messianic psalm about the footsteps of the Anointed, Robertson agrees and applies the title to Jesus, Clarke holds that the Messiah had been revealed to Moses so that opposition to idolatry could be called by that name, Barnes offers three senses and inclines to a technical phrase for sufferings borne in the cause of religion, and Gill allows either Christ personal or Christ mystical

How the beauty of the infant can be a ground of faith: Calvin grants that this seems contrary to the character of faith, and Ellicott answers that the parents took the child’s remarkable beauty as a divine sign given to guide their conduct, while Wesley speaks of a divine presage of things to come

What the recompense Moses looked to was: Wesley denies expressly that it was an inheritance in Canaan, for which Moses had no warrant and which he never attained, and makes it the future happiness his believing ancestors expected, while Robertson says he was laying up treasure in heaven
outliers: Calvin contrasts the parents of Moses with heathens who have saved children at the peril of life merely from a desire of offspring
Robertson traces the word for goodly to the word for a city, so that it means citified or of polished manners
Ellicott dates the refusal precisely to the slaying of the Egyptian, when Moses in act renounced his standing at court
Cyril of Jerusalem argues from this verse and from the spiritual rock that it was Christ whom Moses saw

27.pericope_label: Forsaking Egypt, keeping the passover, passing the Red Sea, the walls of Jericho, and Rahab

schools.summary: Gill takes the forsaking of Egypt of the flight to Midian, since this was before the eating of the passover and so stands in its proper order here, whereas the going out with the children of Israel came after it; the word forsook, he says, implies fleeing, and the occasion was when Pharaoh’s wrath was kindled against him. To the objection that Moses seemed then to be afraid, since he fled, he answers that Moses had shown great courage and intrepidity in slaying the Egyptian and in appearing afterwards among his brethren, and that his withdrawal was a matter of prudence rather than of terror. On the passover he says Moses appointed it by divine direction, kept it with all its rites and ceremonies and caused the people to observe it, doing so in faith of the speedy deliverance of the children of Israel from the house of bondage and in the faith of the Messiah, of whom the passover was a type; and he notes that the Syriac version reads that through faith they kept the passover, that is the Israelites. At the sea he insists that they passed not through a river but through the sea, and argues from the phrase used that they went from one side to the other rather than coming out where they went in, as some say, and that this was all one as if it had been on dry ground, both for Moses and for all the children of Israel; and they did it by faith, believing that God would make a passage quite through it for them. Of Jericho he says the walls fell of themselves and not from any natural cause, reports that the Jews say they sank right down into the ground and were swallowed up, and mentions Kimchi’s observation that perhaps only the portion facing the camp of Israel fell, since Rahab’s house was built upon the wall and yet did not fall. Of Rahab he reports that the Targum calls her a woman that kept a victualling house, a paraphrase noticed by Jarchi and Kimchi who interpret it a seller of food, and that even the Hebrew word is so explained by a considerable Jewish writer; this may rather seem to be the sense of the word and her proper business, both from the spies going to her house as being a house of entertainment and from Salmon’s marrying her, which might otherwise be thought strange. Calvin allows that the forsaking may be said of the first departure as well as of the second, notes that the going out is recorded by the Apostle before the celebration of the passover, and judges that he seems to speak of the flight; nor is the added clause about not fearing any objection to this, though Moses himself relates that he was constrained to flee by fear, for if we look at the beginning of his course the courage was there. Of the passover he says this ought to have availed much to commend faith to the Jews, since they held that first sacrifice in the highest esteem; but it was kept by faith not because the paschal lamb was a type of Christ but because its benefit did not appear when he sprinkled the doorposts with blood, so that when the effect was yet hid it was necessarily looked for by faith. Nay, he adds, it might have seemed strange that Moses should set a few drops of blood as a remedy in opposition to the vengeance of God. At the sea he observes that it is certain many in that multitude were unbelieving, but that the Lord granted to the faith of a few that the whole multitude should pass through dry-shod; and in doing the same thing there was a great difference between the Israelites and the Egyptians, the former passing safely and the latter drowning, the difference arising from nothing but that the Israelites had the word of God and the Egyptians were without it. Of Jericho he says that as he had before taught that the yoke of bondage was by faith broken asunder, so now he tells us that by the same faith the people gained possession of the promised land; at their first entrance the city stood in their way, fortified and almost impregnable, impeding any further progress, and they had no means to assail it, while the command to go round it once every day and seven times on the seventh appeared a work childish and ridiculous. Of Rahab he grants that at first view the example may seem, on account of the meanness of the person, hardly entitled to notice and even unworthy of being recorded, yet it was not unsuitably nor without reason adduced by the Apostle; for he has hitherto shown that the Patriarchs whom the Jews most honoured did nothing worthy of praise except through faith, and now teaches that the same faith avails in one whom the Jews would have despised.

Clarke says of the forsaking that Moses believed God would fulfil the promise he had made and cheerfully changed an earthly for a heavenly portion; and he holds that the apostle speaks here of the departure with the Israelites and not of the flight to Midian, for at that time he was in great fear, whereas when he went to Pharaoh with God’s authority to demand the dismission of the Hebrews he was without fear and acted in the most noble and dignified manner. On the passover he explains that God told Moses he would destroy the first-born of the Egyptians but would spare all those whose doors were sprinkled with the blood of the paschal lamb, and that Moses believed this, kept the passover and sprinkled the blood; he also reports that one of the old Latin copies adds a clause here saying that by faith, when they went out, they spoiled the Egyptians, and dismisses it as anything but genuine. At the sea he draws the contrast sharply: the Egyptians thought they could walk through as well as the Israelites, tried it, and were drowned, while the former passed in perfect safety, the one walking by faith and the other by sight, so that one perished and the other was saved. Of Jericho he says God had promised that the walls should fall down if they compassed them about seven days, and that they believed, did as they were commanded, and the promise was fulfilled. Of Rahab he argues at length that the Hebrew and Greek words which we translate harlot should rather be rendered innkeeper or tavernkeeper, since there is no proper evidence that the person in question was such a woman as our translation represents her; and as to her having been a harlot before and converted afterwards, he calls it a figment of an idle fancy, noting that she was afterwards married into one of the best families in Israel. Wesley says of the forsaking that Moses left Egypt taking all the Israelites with him, and did not then fear the wrath of the king as he had done many years before. Of the passover he notes the pouring out of the blood of the paschal lamb, which was sprinkled on the doorposts lest the destroying angel should touch the Israelites. At the sea he identifies the they as Moses, Aaron and the Israelites, observes that the sea washed the borders of Edom, whose name signifies red, and marks a turn in the chapter, that thus far the examples are cited from Genesis and Exodus while those that follow are from the former and the latter Prophets. Of Rahab he says only that she was formerly one not of the fairest character.

Barnes reports that some have understood the forsaking of the first departure when Moses fled into Midian, but that the majority of expositors suppose it refers to the time when he left Egypt to conduct the Israelites to the promised land; and he holds the latter evident from the fact that it is said he did not fear the wrath of the king, since when Moses first fled to Midian it is expressly said that he went because he feared. On the passover he presses the Greek, which says that he made the passover, meaning more, it seems to him, than that he merely kept or celebrated it: it implies that he instituted the rite and made the arrangements for its observance, with reference to his special agency and the special faith he had in its institution, the faith in the case being confidence that this would be the means of preserving the firstborn of the Israelites when the angel should destroy the firstborn of the Egyptians. At the sea he says it was only by confidence in God that they were able to pass, not by any power they had to remove the waters or make a passage for themselves, and not by the operation of any natural causes; it is not to be supposed that all who passed through the Red Sea had saving faith, the assertion being that the passage was made in virtue of strong confidence in God. Of Jericho he says it was not by any natural causes or by any means in themselves adapted to secure such a result: not because the walls fell of themselves, nor because they were assailed by the hosts of the Israelites, nor because there was any natural tendency in the blowing of horns to cause them to fall; none of these things were true, and it was only by confidence in God that means so little adapted to such a purpose could produce it. Of Rahab he recounts that she resided in Jericho, that when Joshua crossed the Jordan he sent two men as spies to her house and she saved them by concealment from the enemies that would have destroyed their lives, and that for this act of hospitality and kindness they assured her of safety when the city should be destroyed and directed her to give an indication of her place of abode that her house might be spared. Ellicott calls the question of the forsaking a matter of great difficulty, and reports that the view referring it to the flight into Midian seems to be taken by all ancient writers and by most in modern times, supported by three arguments: that the institution of the Passover is mentioned later in this chapter, that the second departure was made at Pharaoh’s urgent request, and that the verb rendered he forsook is too personal an expression for the national departure. On the passover he prefers by faith he hath kept, as elsewhere in the chapter, and says the celebration and the sprinkling of the blood were acts of obedience having reference to a danger as yet unseen but present in God’s word; the following clause he renders that the destroyer of the first-born may not touch them. At the sea he renders the clause literally as of which the Egyptians making trial were swallowed up, and observes that in the same trial, but with the support of the word of God, had consisted Israel’s faith; he notes that the word land is absent from the ordinary Greek text though found in the best manuscripts. Of Jericho he brings into relief the persistence of Israel’s obedience during the seven days of almost total inaction, in the midst, we cannot doubt, of the unmeasured contempt and ridicule of their foes. Of the men of Jericho he prefers that they were disobedient to that they believed not, and observes that to Rahab and to her countrymen alike had come the knowledge of what the Lord had done for Israel; she recognised from these signs and acknowledged the supremacy of the Lord and cast in her lot with his servants, while the men of Jericho continued in their disobedience and perished, so that through faith a despised heathen woman became united with the people of God. Robertson parses the negative with the first aorist passive participle used transitively, notes that Moses did flee from Egypt after slaying the Egyptian but that the author omits that slaughter and ignores it as the dominant motive in the flight, and parses the following verb as a constative aorist of an old word meaning to be steadfast. On the passover he takes the perfect as emphasising the permanent nature of the feast, and renders the second phrase rather as the pouring of the blood, from a verb meaning to pour upon, occurring only here in the New Testament and the earliest known example of the noun, alluding to the command in Exodus though the Greek Old Testament uses the verb regularly for the act. At the sea he renders the idiom literally as taking trial of which, notes that it occurs in the Greek Old Testament and in the New only here and later in the chapter though it is a classical idiom, and parses the following verb as a first aorist passive of a verb meaning to drink down or swallow down. Of Jericho he parses the aorist of falling with first aorist endings and the participle of encircling as marking antecedent action. Of Rahab he parses the first aorist middle participle of the verb to welcome, and glosses the word for spies as an old compound used of a scout or spy, found in the Greek Old Testament and here only in the New.

Chrysostom pauses over the manner of the writer rather than the matter. Paul, he says, is wont to establish many things incidentally and is very full of thoughts, for such is the grace of the Spirit: he does not comprehend a few ideas in a multitude of words but includes great and manifold thought in brevity of expressions. He then applies the observation to this very verse, bidding the reader observe how, in the midst of exhortation and when discoursing about faith, the writer reminds them of a type and a mystery whereof they themselves have the reality; for in saying that through faith Moses kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood so that the destroyer should not touch them, he sets before Christian readers the figure of what they possess in the blood of Christ. The point for Chrysostom is that the argument about faith and the doctrine of redemption are not two separate subjects laid side by side, but that the one carries the other, so that even an incidental clause in a list of examples turns out to contain the whole mystery in small compass.

debates: Whether the forsaking of Egypt is the flight to Midian or the Exodus: Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all take it of the departure with the people, chiefly because the text says Moses did not fear the king whereas the flight is expressly ascribed to fear, while Ellicott reports that all ancient writers and most moderns take it of the flight and adds three arguments, that the Passover is mentioned only afterwards, that the second departure was made at Pharaoh’s own request, and that the verb is too personal for a national exodus; Gill argues from the same order and Calvin leans the same way while allowing either

Whether faith was needed to keep the passover at all: Calvin insists that the act was one of faith not because the lamb was a type of Christ but because its benefit was wholly hidden at the time, and remarks how strange it must have seemed to set a few drops of blood against so great a destruction, while Barnes finds the faith rather in the institution of the rite than in its observance

What Rahab was: Clarke argues that the Hebrew and Greek words rendered harlot should be rendered innkeeper, denies any evidence for the usual reading and calls the story of a later conversion a figment of an idle fancy, and Gill supports the same sense from the Targum and from Jarchi and Kimchi, while Wesley keeps the traditional description in a phrase and Calvin defends the example precisely on the ground of the meanness of the person
outliers: Chrysostom takes the passing mention of the sprinkled blood as an incidental clause carrying the whole mystery of redemption
Calvin explains the difference between Israel and Egypt at the sea by nothing but the possession of the word of God
Ellicott stresses seven days of almost total inaction under the ridicule of the defenders
Gill reports the rabbinic tradition that the walls sank into the ground, and notes that Rahab’s house stood on the wall and did not fall

32.pericope_label: What shall I more say: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening question as intimating that the writer had said enough to prove the definition of faith he had given, and that the elders by it had obtained a good report, and yet that he had not said all he could, having so much to say that he could not say all. On the subduing of kingdoms he instances David in particular, who subdued Syria, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, Edom and the Philistines, and draws two conclusions from the clause: that war in some cases is lawful and kingdoms may be subdued, faith making use of means to do it, though these kingdoms, subdued by faith, were not subdued without fighting; and that believers therefore have no reason to be afraid of kings or kingdoms, which should encourage the saints in their combats with the powers of darkness. On the quenching of fire he lists the ways in which it may be said to be done: when a believer or a righteous man is delivered out of it, as Lot from Sodom when God rained fire and brimstone upon it; when by prayer it is stopped, as by Moses at Taberah; when persons are not hurt by it, as the three Hebrews cast into Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace; and, he adds, many of the martyrs have triumphed in the flames. He then turns each clause into a spiritual application: believers are delivered out of the fire of afflictions and are not consumed thereby, they quench the fiery darts of Satan thrown at them, they are untouched by the fire of God’s wrath in every state and case, and they shall not be hurt of the second death, which is a lake of fire burning with brimstone. Calvin explains why the writer changes his method here. As it was to be feared that by referring to a few examples he should appear to confine the praises of faith to a few men, he anticipates this and says that there would be no end if he was to dwell on every instance, for what he had said of a few extended to the whole Church of God. He notes that the writer first refers to the time that intervened between Joshua and David, when the Lord raised up judges to govern the people, and that such were the four now mentioned. He then dwells on how unpromising each of them was: it seemed strange to attack an immense host of enemies with three hundred men, and to shake pitchers appeared like a sham alarm; the second was far inferior to his enemies and was guided only by the counsel of a woman; the third was a mere countryman who had never used arms. On the raising up from weakness he reports that an older interpreter referred the clause to the restoration of the Jews from exile, in which they were like men without hope, says he does not disapprove of the application to Hezekiah, and adds that we might at the same time extend it wider, that the Lord by his hand raised on high his saints whenever they were cast down and brought help to their weakness so as to endue them with full strength.

Henry observes that the apostle, having given a class of many eminent believers whose names are mentioned and the particular trials and actings of whose faith are recorded, now concludes his narrative with a more summary account of another set of believers, where the particular acts are not ascribed to particular persons by name but left to be applied by those who are well acquainted with the sacred story. Like a divine orator, he says, the writer prefaces this part of the narrative with an elegant expostulation, as if he had said that it is in vain to attempt to exhaust this subject, and that should he not restrain his pen it would soon run beyond the bounds of an epistle, so that he will but just mention the names of some of the rest. Henry then takes the summary as showing what faith enables men to do and to bear across every kind of condition: some are named who wrought great deliverances for the nation, others who suffered greatly and were not delivered at all, and the same principle is at work in both. He presses on the reader that the roll is left deliberately open, the writer naming the men but leaving their achievements unassigned, so that those who know the history may fit each clause to its person and be the more affected for having made the application themselves; and he draws from the whole the encouragement that the God who supported such a variety of persons under such a variety of trials is the same God to whom his readers may look in their own.

Clarke explains the opening as a very usual mode of expression with the best Greek writers, used when they wish to intimate that much important intelligence remains to be communicated on the subject in hand which must be omitted because of other points not yet handled. He then gives a brief account of each man named: the first by faith in God with three hundred men destroyed a countless multitude of Midianites and Amalekites and delivered Israel from oppression and slavery; the second overthrew Jabin king of Canaan and delivered Israel from servitude; the third was appointed by God to deliver Israel from the oppressive yoke of the Philistines and by extraordinary assistance discomfited them. On the subduing of kingdoms he instances Joshua, who subdued the seven Canaanitish nations, and David, who subdued the Moabites, Syrians, Ammonites and Edomites; on the working of righteousness, a great variety of works indicative of that faith in God without which it is impossible to do anything that is good; and on the obtaining of promises he supposes a reference to Joshua and Caleb, who through their faith in God obtained the promised land while all the rest of the Israelites were excluded, to Phinehas, who for his act of zealous faith got the promise of an everlasting priesthood, and to David, who for his faith and obedience obtained the kingdom of Israel. On the quenching of fire he names the three faithful Hebrews who for their steady attachment to God’s worship were cast into a fiery furnace, in which they were preserved and from which they escaped unhurt; on escaping the sword, Moses who escaped the sword of Pharaoh, Elijah that of Jezebel, and David that of Saul, and many others; on being made strong out of weakness, those miraculously restored from sickness which seemed to threaten their life, as Hezekiah; and on waxing valiant in fight, Gideon who overthrew the camp of the Midianites and Jonathan that of the Philistines, in such a way as must have proved that God was with them. Wesley notes the ordering of the names, that after Samuel the prophets are properly mentioned, that David also was a prophet though he was a king too, and that the prophets meant are Elijah and Elisha and the rest, including likewise the believers who lived with them. He then distributes the clauses that follow among the persons named: David in particular subdued kingdoms, Samuel, not excluding the rest, wrought righteousness, and the prophets in general obtained promises both for themselves and to deliver to others; prophets also stopped the mouths of lions, as Daniel, and quenched the violence of fire, as Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. To these examples, whence the nature of faith clearly appears, he observes that the more ancient ones are subjoined by a transposition and in an inverted order, and receive light from these: Jephthah escaped the edge of the sword, Samson out of weakness was made strong, Barak became valiant in fight, Gideon put to flight armies of the aliens. He closes with the general reflection that faith animates to the most heroic enterprises, both civil and military.

Barnes says there are numerous other instances showing the strength of faith which there is not time to mention, and that the writer means he cannot recount all that they did or all the illustrations of the power of faith evinced in their lives. He gives a short notice of each name, observing of the first that there can be no doubt he was sustained and animated in his wars by strong confidence in God, and of the second that at the command of the prophetess who summoned him to war in the name of the Lord he encountered and overthrew the hosts of Sisera, his yielding to her summons and his valour in battle showing that he was influenced by faith. On the clauses that follow he explains that some of them subdued kingdoms and others obtained promises, instancing Joshua who subdued the nations of Canaan, Gideon the Midianites, Jephthah the Ammonites, and David the Philistines and Amalekites and Edomites; the working of righteousness he takes as carrying the laws of justice into execution, particularly on guilty nations, so that they executed the great purposes of God in punishing the wicked. The obtaining of promises he takes, with Bloomfield and Stuart, as obtaining promised blessings, that is, receiving as a result of their faith promises of blessing on their posterity in future times. On the later clauses he names the three Hebrews for the quenching of fire; for escaping the sword, Elijah fleeing from Ahab, Elisha delivered from the king of Syria, and David fleeing from Saul; and for being made strong out of weakness, either those enabled to perform exploits beyond their natural strength, such as Samson, or those raised from bodily infirmity and invigorated for conflict, such as Hezekiah restored from dangerous sickness by the immediate interposition of God. Ellicott observes that the sacred writer has lingered over the life and deeds of the greatest of the patriarchs and of Moses the legislator of the nation, and that two examples only, differing in kind from those which preceded and peculiarly suggestive, have been taken from the history of the people after the death of Moses; enough has now been said, he judges, to guide all who are willing to search the Scriptures for themselves, and with a brief mention of names which would call up before the minds of his readers achievements almost as wonderful as those on which he has been dwelling, the writer passes from the elders who received witness from God by their faith and speaks in general terms of what faith has done and suffered. He prefers overcame kingdoms to subdued kingdoms and applies the words to all the deliverers of Israel just named and especially to David, noting that they also wrought righteousness, as each judge or king or prophet executed judgment and justice unto all his people. On the promises he asks whether the words mean that these men of faith won promises of future blessing, such as were vouchsafed to David and the prophets, or that promises of deliverance were fulfilled to them, and answers that there seems no reason for doubting that the writer’s language may include both thoughts. On the later clauses he prefers the power of fire to the violence of fire, and though it would not be difficult to trace the application of these clauses to the heroes of Israel celebrated in the Old Testament history, since the perils of David and Elijah and the weakness of Samson and Hezekiah will occur to the mind of all, he judges it likely that the writer’s thought is resting mainly on the history of the Maccabean times, since the following verse is generally acknowledged to relate to narratives contained in the second book of Maccabees and no words could more truly characterise the general contents of the first book than those of the present verse. Robertson parses the opening question as a deliberative present active subjunctive and calls it both a literary and an oratorical idiom, the writer feeling helpless to go on in the same style as he has done from Abel to Rahab; the following clause he renders literally as will leave me telling about, a vivid and picturesque description of the author’s embarrassment of riches as he contemplates the long list of the heroes of faith, and he notes that the participle is masculine, which disposes of Priscilla as a possible author. The first verb of the next verse he parses as a first aorist middle of a compound occurring here alone in the New Testament and used by Josephus of David’s conquests. He observes that the writer here has, in Moffatt’s phrase, nine terse clauses with no connective at all, and finds in this asyndeton great rhetorical and oratorical force, calling it a sledge-hammer style. Of the individual clauses he notes the second aorist of the verb to flee, renders the phrase as mouths of the sword, parses the passive of a late verb for being made strong, renders the next as became strong in battle, and glosses the last noun as a late compound used for an encampment, for barracks, and for armies drawn up in battle line.

debates: What obtaining promises means: Ellicott asks whether these men won promises of future blessing, such as were given to David and the prophets, or whether promises of deliverance were fulfilled to them, and answers that the language may well include both, while Barnes follows Bloomfield and Stuart in taking it of promised blessings on their posterity, and Clarke assigns particular promises to Joshua and Caleb, to Phinehas and to David

Whether the closing clauses look back to Israel’s history or forward to the Maccabees: Ellicott grants that the perils of David and Elijah and the weakness of Samson and Hezekiah come readily to mind, but judges that the writer’s thought rests mainly on the Maccabean period, since the next verse is generally acknowledged to draw on the second book and these words characterise the contents of the first

What being made strong out of weakness refers to: Calvin reports an older application to the restoration of the Jews from exile, allows the application to Hezekiah, and would extend the clause wider to every raising up of the saints, while Barnes divides it between exploits beyond natural strength and recovery from bodily infirmity
outliers: Robertson counts nine terse clauses set down without a connective and calls the effect a sledge-hammer style
Robertson notes that the masculine participle rules out Priscilla as the author of the epistle
