Calvin dwells on the unlikeliness of the instruments, three hundred men, shaken pitchers, a leader guided by a woman, and a countryman who had never borne arms
Gill infers from the clause about subduing kingdoms that war is in some cases lawful and that believers need not fear kings

35.pericope_label: Tortured, mocked, stoned, sawn asunder: of whom the world was not worthy

schools.summary: Gill names the two women who received their dead raised, the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite, and observes that their sons were really dead and that they received them alive again from the hands of the prophets Elijah and Elisha in the way of a resurrection, and by faith, that is by the faith of the prophets. Of the mockings he gives instances: Samson mocked by the Philistines, Elisha by the children whom the bears devoured, Jeremiah by Pashur and others, the Jews by Sanballat and Tobiah when building, and the prophets whom God sent to the Jews as his messengers. Of the stoning he names Naboth, put to death by the order of Ahab, and Zechariah slain in the court of the Lord’s house, and recalls that the character given to Jerusalem is that she stoned the prophets that were sent to her. On the parenthesis he explains why it stands where it does: the words are inserted to remove or prevent such objections as that these men were restless and unquiet persons who made disturbance in the world and so were unfit to live in it, and that they were deservedly punished for crimes they were guilty of; and they serve to show the great worth and inestimable value of the people of God, which exceeds that of the whole world, intimating that their removal out of the world, or from dwelling among the men of it, is itself by way of punishment to the world. Calvin observes that having already mentioned instances in which God remunerated the faith of his servants, the writer now refers to examples of a different kind, that saints reduced to extreme miseries struggled by faith so as to persevere invincible even to death. These instances, he grants, at first view widely differ: some triumphed gloriously over vanquished enemies, were preserved by the Lord through various miracles and were rescued by means new and unusual from the midst of death, while others were shamefully treated, were despised by almost the whole world, were consumed by want and were so hated by all as to be compelled to hide themselves. Yet he insists that the same faith is at work in both, since it belongs to faith as much to bear as to prevail. On the parenthesis he says that as the holy Prophets wandered as fugitives among wild beasts they might have seemed unworthy of being sustained on the earth, for how was it that they could find no place among men? But the Apostle inverts this sentiment and says that the world was not worthy of them, for wherever God’s servants come they bring with them his blessing like the fragrance of a sweet odour. Thus the house of Potiphar was blessed for Joseph’s sake, and Sodom would have been spared had ten righteous men been found in it; and though the world may cast out God’s servants as offscourings, it is yet preserved for their sake.

Clarke names the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite for the raising of the dead, and adds honestly that what other cases under all the above heads the apostle might have in view, we know not. On the word rendered tortured he says the critics are not agreed about its meaning: the root signifies a stick or baton which was used in bastinadoing criminals, and the verb signifies to beat violently, being thus explained by the best lexicographers; after considering what others have written on the subject he is inclined to think that the bastinado on the soles of the feet is what is here meant. Of the mockings he says we do not know the cases to which the apostle refers, but that they can never mean such things as those of Ishmael against Isaac or the youths of Bethel against Elisha; it is more probable that the reference is to public exhibitions of the people of God at idol feasts and the like, and Samson’s case before Dagon, when the Philistines had put out his eyes, is quite in point. As to scourgings, he observes that this was a common way of punishing minor culprits, and that even those who were to be punished capitally were first scourged, as in the case of our Lord. On the stoning he names Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, slain between the altar and the temple, and Naboth the Jezreelite, who on refusing to give up his father’s inheritance to a covetous king, because it had respect to the promise of God, was falsely accused and stoned to death. On the sawing asunder he reports the tradition that the prophet Isaiah was thus martyred, and quotes the Talmudic account that Manasseh slew Isaiah, commanding that he should be slain with a wooden saw. On the parenthesis he says that these men, of whom the world was not worthy, were yet obliged to wander by day in deserts and mountains, driven from the society of men, and often obliged to hide by night in dens and caves of the earth to conceal themselves from the brutal rage of men; and he suggests that the writer refers here principally to the case of Elijah and of the hundred prophets hidden in caves by Obadiah and fed with bread and water, adding that David also was often obliged to hide himself from Saul. Wesley notes that the women were naturally weak and that the dead they received were their children, and marks the movement of the passage, that from those who acted great things the apostle rises higher, to those who showed the power of faith by suffering. The deliverance refused he explains as deliverance offered on sinful terms, and the better resurrection as a higher reward, seeing that the greater their sufferings the greater would be their glory. Of the later verses he observes that the apostle seems to pass on to recent examples, reports the Jewish tradition that Isaiah was sawn asunder by Manasseh, and resolves the difficulty of the word rendered tempted by the arrangement of the list: torments and death are mentioned alternately, so that they were tried every way, by threatenings, reproaches and tortures the variety of which cannot be expressed, and again by promises and allurements. On the parenthesis he says the world did not deserve so great a blessing, and that they wandered being driven out from men.

Barnes names the woman of Zarephath whose child was restored by Elijah and the Shunammite whose child was restored by Elisha. The word rendered tortured he derives from the noun for a drum, tabret or timbrel, the instrument in the East consisting of a thin wooden rim covered over with skin, and explains that the form of severe torture so named was probably called after it from the resemblance. Of the mockings he says the reference is to the scorn and derision which the ancient victims of persecution experienced, as martyrs have often experienced since, and that some instances are mentioned in the Old Testament while it was frequent in the time of the Maccabees. Scourging he calls a common mode of punishment usually inflicted before a martyr was put to death. Of the stoning he says it was a common method of punishment among the Jews, instances Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, and thinks it not improbable that this was often resorted to in times of popular tumult, as in the case of Stephen, and that such instances probably occurred also under Antiochus Epiphanes and under Manasseh. On the sawing asunder he reports the common supposition that Isaiah was put to death in this manner. On the parenthesis he says the world was so wicked that it had no claim that such holy men should live in it, these poor and despised and persecuted men, living as outcasts and wanderers, being of a character far elevated above the world; the expression he calls a most beautiful one, at once a statement of their eminent holiness and of the wickedness of the rest of mankind, and the following words a description of persons driven away from their homes and wandering from place to place to procure a scanty subsistence. Ellicott renders the phrase about the women literally as by a resurrection, and marks the turn in the chapter: at this point the character of the record is changed, for hitherto we have heard of the victories of faith in action and now it is of the triumph of faith over suffering that the writer speaks, so that those who escaped the edge of the sword and those who were slain with the sword alike exemplified the power of faith. For the torture he points to the account of the aged Eleazar, martyred because he would not pollute himself with swine’s flesh and with flesh taken from the sacrifice commanded by the king. Of the later clauses he says the language becomes more general but still refers chiefly to the same troublous times, and calls the bonds a lasting and cruel captivity, a worse fate even than mockings and scourgings. On the stoning he names Zechariah and, according to a Jewish tradition mentioned by Tertullian and others, Jeremiah; on the sawing asunder he reports an ancient tradition mentioned both by Jewish and by early Christian writers that Isaiah was thus put to death by order of Manasseh. The following words about being tempted he calls very remarkable in such a position, notes that many conjectures have been hazarded on the supposition that a mistake of transcription has occurred, and holds that if the text is correct the writer is speaking of the promises and allurements by which the persecuted were assailed. Robertson parses the phrase for the resurrection of the women’s children, and takes the verb for torturing as a first aorist passive of a late verb formed from the word for a kettledrum or drumstick, meaning to beat the drum and so to beat to death, comparing the account of Eleazar and the mother and her seven sons and noting that the verb occurs once in the Greek Old Testament. The deliverance refused he says was offered at the price of disloyalty, and the clause about the better resurrection he parses as a purpose clause with the second aorist subjunctive of the verb to obtain. Of the mockings he notes that the noun is a late word found in the Greek Old Testament and here alone in the New, while the word for scourges is old and common. On the stoning he cites Zechariah the son of Jehoiada and calls it a characteristic Jewish punishment; the sawing asunder he calls a cruel Jewish punishment said to have been inflicted on Isaiah; and of the following word he observes that the manuscripts vary greatly in the text here and in the order of these two items, and that this mild word seems an anticlimax after the sawing. On the parenthesis he calls it a graphic picture in a short parenthetical relative clause, a phrase to stir the blood of the readers, parses the participle of wandering as a present middle and compares lost sheep hunted by wolves, and glosses the words for caves and holes as old terms, the latter occurring in the New Testament only here and in the epistle of James.

Chrysostom turns the passage upon himself and his hearers before he expounds it. At all times indeed, he says, but especially when he reflects upon the achievements of the saints, it comes over him to feel despondency concerning his own condition, because we have not even in dreams experienced the things among which those men spent their whole lives. The sting of the comparison for him lies in a distinction he draws sharply: those men were not paying the penalty of sins, as we might be if we suffered, but were always doing rightly and yet were always afflicted, so that their sufferings cannot be explained away as chastisement and stand simply as the cost of faithfulness. He then fixes on the particular figure to whom the discourse has come round, Elijah, of whom the writer speaks in this passage and with whom his examples end, and finds the choice appropriate to the readers’ case; and having spoken of what befell the Apostles, that they were slain with the sword, he sets the prophet beside them, wandering in sheepskins and goatskins on the mountains, so that the whole line of the persecuted from the prophets to the Apostles is shown to be one company under one discipline.

debates: What the word rendered tortured describes: Barnes derives it from the drum or timbrel and takes it of a torture named after the instrument, Robertson likewise makes it beating the drum and so beating to death, while Clarke reports that the critics are not agreed, traces the root to the baton used in bastinadoing criminals, and after weighing the alternatives inclines to the bastinado on the soles of the feet

What to make of the word rendered tempted: Ellicott calls it very remarkable in such a position, reports many conjectures resting on the supposition of a scribal error, and holds that if the text stands the writer means the promises and allurements used against the persecuted, Robertson notes that the manuscripts vary greatly in reading and order and calls the mild word an anticlimax after the sawing asunder, while Wesley resolves it from the arrangement, that torments and enticements are named alternately

Whether the closing clauses look to the Old Testament or to the Maccabean period: Ellicott points to the aged Eleazar and to the troublous times of the persecution, Barnes allows both the older instances and those under Antiochus Epiphanes, and Robertson cites the mother and her seven sons alongside Zechariah
outliers: Calvin inverts the natural judgment, that the world is preserved for the sake of the men it casts out, as Potiphar’s house was blessed for Joseph and Sodom would have been spared for ten
Clarke reports the Talmudic account that Manasseh had Isaiah sawn with a wooden saw
Robertson describes the wanderers as lost sheep hunted by wolves
Chrysostom confesses despondency at the comparison, since these men suffered while always doing rightly

39.pericope_label: These all received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us

schools.summary: Gill allows the phrase to be taken two ways. It may be limited to the sufferers in the preceding verses, who were martyred or suffered martyrdom for the faith, as the words may be rendered, and who are called martyrs or witnesses, the Ethiopic version rendering the clause that all these were witnesses concerning the faith; or it may be extended to all the instances of faith throughout the chapter, so that the apostle here reasserts what he had said at the beginning, having proved it by a variety of examples. On the better thing he is careful to exclude the obvious candidates: it is not a better state of the church in such respect as to be free from suffering reproach and persecutions, for this is the case of saints under the New Testament as under the Old; nor the felicity of the soul after death; nor any greater degree of happiness in the other world; nor the perfection of blessedness in soul and body, these being things common to all believers. It is Christ, as now exhibited in the flesh. Jesus Christ, he insists, was the same in the yesterday of the Old Testament as he is in the present day of the Gospel dispensation, being slain from the foundation of the world, and the saints then were saved as now by his grace and righteousness; only with this difference between them and us, that they had Christ in the promise while we have him himself that was promised, and they had him in type and shadow while we have him in reality and truth. Calvin reads the conclusion as an argument from the less to the greater: if they on whom the light of grace had not as yet so brightly shone displayed so great a constancy in enduring evils, what ought the full brightness of the Gospel to produce in us? A small spark of light led them to heaven; when the sun of righteousness shines over us, with what pretence can we excuse ourselves if we still cleave to the earth? This, he says, is the real meaning of the Apostle. He reports that Beza, Doddridge, Scott and Stuart take the view that the promise is especially that of Christ, the ancients having heard of him and believed in his coming but not witnessed it, and that the better thing is the same with the promise, or the Gospel as revealed, or in Stuart’s words the actual fulfilment of the promise respecting the Messiah; but he adds that there is still something unsatisfactory in this view, and presses rather the practical comparison between their light and ours, which is where he takes the force of the passage to lie.

Henry turns the closing verses into an argument against his readers. The world considers that the righteous are not worthy to live in the world, and God declares that the world is not worthy of them; and though the righteous and the worldlings widely differ in their judgment, they agree in this, that it is not fit that good men should have their rest in this world, and therefore God receives them out of it. He then presses the inference from the better provision: the apostle tells the Hebrews that God had provided some better things for them, and therefore they might be sure that he expected as good things from them. As our advantages, with the better things God has provided for us, are so much beyond theirs, so should our obedience of faith, our patience of hope and our labour of love be greater; and unless we get true faith as these believers had, they will rise up to condemn us at the last day. He closes with the exhortation that we should pray continually for the increase of our faith, that we may follow these bright examples and be at length made perfect with them.

Clarke explains the good report as having been witnessed to, and says it was faith in God which supported all those eminent men who in different parts of the world and in different ages were persecuted for righteousness’ sake. On what they did not receive he is exact: they all heard of the promises made to Abraham of a heavenly rest and of the promise of the Messiah, for this was a constant tradition, but they died without having seen this Anointed of the Lord, since Christ was not in any of their times manifested in the flesh, and of him who was the expectation of all nations they heard only by the hearing of the ear; this must be the promise, without receiving of which the apostle says they died. The better thing he identifies as the dispensation of the Gospel with all the privileges and advantages it confers. On the last clause he sets out a doctrine of the one Church: believers before the flood, after the flood, under the law and since the law make but one Church; the Gospel dispensation is the last, and the Church cannot be considered as complete till the believers under all dispensations are gathered together, so that the preceding believers cannot be consummated even in glory till the Gospel Church arrives in the heaven of heavens. He grants that a great variety of meanings have been put on the place but judges this the most simple and consistent, and supports it from the vision in which white robes were given to every one of the martyrs and it was said to them that they should rest yet for a little season until their fellow servants and their brethren should be fulfilled. Wesley says that though they obtained a good testimony they did not receive the great promise, the heavenly inheritance; the better thing he names as everlasting glory, and the last clause he explains as meaning that we might all be perfected together in heaven.

Barnes says they were all commended and approved on account of their confidence in God, and that they did not receive the fulfilment of the promise, or did not receive all that was promised, still looking forward to some future blessings. On the better thing he explains that God had provided, or determined on giving, some better thing than any of them realised and which we are now permitted to enjoy: God gave them promises but they were not allowed to see their fulfilment, whereas we are permitted now to see what those promises referred to and in part at least to witness their completion, so that though the promise was made to them the fulfilment more particularly pertains to us. On the last clause he reasons from the system rather than from the persons: the whole system of revelation was not complete at once, or in one generation, but required successive ages to make it complete, so that it might be said to be finished or perfect; our existence, therefore, and the developments in our times, were as necessary to the perfection of the system as the promise made to the patriarchs, and the patriarchs could not be made perfect without the later ages any more than the later ages without them. Ellicott observes that now the history is concluded the word used at the beginning of the chapter is resumed, and that the records themselves have shown how in such a faith as was described at the outset the elders received their witness from God; yet these all, having had witness borne to them through their faith, received not the promise, that is the promised blessing. He sets three passages of the epistle side by side which must be kept together: the statement that Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise; the exhortation that the readers have need of endurance, that having done the will of God they may receive the promise; and the present verse. To the saints of the Old Testament, he concludes, the promised blessing was future; they obtained it, but not within the limits of this present life, whereas to us the promised blessing is present, revealed in its true nature and obtained for us once for all. On the last verse he prefers rendering the preposition concerning us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect, and defines the better thing as better than they had received. The design of God, he says, was that they and we may be perfected together, first in the joint reception of mature knowledge and privilege through the high-priestly work of the Lord Jesus, and then that we with them may, when the end shall come, have our perfect consummation and bliss both in body and soul in the eternal and everlasting glory of God. Robertson takes the phrase of the whole list from the beginning of the chapter, notes that the preposition is used here rather than the simple dative as so often, and parses the verb as a first aorist middle; the Messianic promise, he says, they did not live to see, though they had individual special promises fulfilled as already shown. On the last verse he parses the genitive absolute with the first aorist middle participle of a late compound meaning to foresee, occurring here only in the New Testament, identifies the better thing as the better promises named earlier in the epistle, and parses the negative purpose clause with the first aorist passive subjunctive. He then adds a caution: this glorious and gracious purpose of God is not due to any special merit in us but is simply the fulness of the time in God’s dispensation of grace, of which we are the beneficiaries; but all the same, and all the more, we should prove worthy of our heritage and of God’s goodness to us, and be loyal to Christ.

debates: What the promise was that they did not receive: Clarke identifies it as the manifestation of the Messiah in the flesh, of whom they heard only by the hearing of the ear, Robertson likewise distinguishes the Messianic promise from the individual promises that were fulfilled to them, Wesley calls it the heavenly inheritance, and Ellicott sets the verse against two earlier passages to show that the blessing was obtained but not within this life

What the better thing provided for us is: Gill excludes freedom from persecution, the felicity of the soul after death, and any greater degree of happiness hereafter, and identifies it as Christ exhibited in the flesh, so that the difference is between having him in promise and having him that was promised, while Clarke makes it the Gospel dispensation with its privileges, Robertson the better promises, and Wesley everlasting glory

Why the earlier saints could not be perfected without us: Clarke argues that all believers of every dispensation form one Church which cannot be complete until the last of them is gathered, and supports it from the martyrs told to rest a little season, while Barnes reasons instead from the system of revelation, which required successive ages to be finished, and Ellicott from a joint perfecting through the high-priestly work of Christ
outliers: Calvin turns the whole chapter into an argument from the less to the greater: a small spark of light led them to heaven, and the sun of righteousness now shines over us
Henry warns that these believers will rise up to condemn us at the last day if we lack the faith they had
Gill states the difference between the two dispensations as promise against fulfilment, type and shadow against reality and truth
Robertson cautions that the better provision reflects no merit in us but only the fulness of the time
